question: During canine CT angiographic evaluation of congenital extrahepatic portosystemic shunts, how should a shunt running from the splenic vein to the prehepatic caudal vena cava and another arising from the right gastric vein be named under the Nelson and Nelson versus White and Parry classification systems?
A: Nelson and Nelson: splenocaval and right gastrocaval; White and Parry: left gastrocaval and right gastric type Ai.
B: Nelson and Nelson: left gastrocaval and right gastric type Ai; White and Parry: splenocaval and right gastrocaval.
C: Nelson and Nelson: splenoazygos and right gastroazygos; White and Parry: left gastric type Bi and right gastric type Bii.
D: Nelson and Nelson: portocaval and gastrophrenic; White and Parry: central divisional intrahepatic and right divisional intrahepatic.
Contextual materials: CT and VR are widely used tools in the diagnosis, classification, and surgical planning of CEPSs. In the present study, we identified a deviation originating in the splenic vein and inserted in the pre-hepatic caudal vena cava in one case, and another shunt coming from the right gastric vein, according to the main classifications available for CEPSs. According to Nelson and Nelson’s classification, these types of deviations are called splenocaval and right gastrocaval, while according to White and Parry, they are named left gastrocaval and right gastric of type Ai. Segmentation was carried out using the free 3D Slicer software, which, even though it was effective, had some limitations regarding the individualized segmentation of the liver lobes and the automated segmentation of the blood vessels. Paid software offers a greater variety of tools and user support, and has been widely used in similar studies, such as OsiriX (Pixmeo, Sarl, Geneva, Switzerland), Materialise Mimics (Materialise, Leuven, Belgium), Vitrea (Canon Medical Systems Corporation, Otawara, Japan), Dicom to print (3D Systems Inc., Rock Hill, SC, USA), Avizo (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA), ScanIP (Synopsys, Sunnyvale, CA, USA), AMIRA (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA), Terarecon (Terarecon, Durham, NC, USA), ZedView (LEXI, Chuo-Ku, Tokyo, Japan), M3DICS (M3DICS, Turin, Italy), Volume Extractor (i-Plants Systems, Iwate-ken, Takizawa, Japan), and other non-paid software such as InVesalius (CenPRA, Campinas, São Paulo, Brazil), ITK-SNAP (University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA, USA), Seg3D (University of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT, USA), and Freesurfer (Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, MA, USA). Commercial software is generally better than free software and provides customer support. As a non-paid alternative, InVesalius was also tested before the beginning of this study; however, it was not selected for use since it showed an inferior performance to 3D Slicer, even on a computer with technical specifications higher than recommended.

question: When the ventral synovial fold of the canine atlantoaxial joint is examined histologically across mediolateral locations in relation to the dens axis, which finding is most consistent with the regional pattern of its subintimal stroma?
A: At the level of the dens, the ventral fold is predominantly adipose, with abundant fat lobules and only sparse collagen strands.
B: At the level of the dens, the ventral fold is predominantly fibrous, with densely packed fibrous strands and relatively poor vascularity.
C: Lateral to the dens, the middle portion of the ventral fold is predominantly areolar, with loose connective tissue and minimal axial fiber organization.
D: In the peripheral atlantoaxial joint, the ventral fold remains uniformly fibrous, with no transition toward adipose tissue.
Contextual materials: Notably, the shape of the canine synovial fold, especially the ventral fold permitted subdivision into three parts: (1) base, (2) middle, (3) apex, corresponding to the observation in humans. In addition, we were able to assign the three types of subintimal stroma described in humans—areolar, fibrous and adipose—to the canine synovial folds on the basis of the tissue composition. The synovial folds in this study were described at diferent levels of the atlantoaxial joint and, interestingly, the composition of the subintimal stroma varied depending on the location in the joint. At the level of the dens axis the subintima of the ventral synovial fold showed characteristics of the fibrous type with densely packed fibrous strands and poor vasculature. Although the subintima of the large ventral fold in the area lateral to the dens axis had fibrous strands at the base which were more loosely packed and more vascularized than the fibers of the fold at the level of the dens axis, the middle part of the fold in particular consisted of densely packed, almost axially arranged fibers representing the fibrous type. Sections of the ventral fold at a more lateral level and in the periphery of the atlantoaxial joint exhibited features consistent with the adipose type. Studies of synovial folds in humans have also described mixed forms of the various characteristic types, such as the fibroadipose type, and the subintimal stroma also regularly contains blood vessels, nerve fibers, lymphatic vessels and elastic fibers. However, it is not yet clear from the literature whether the mixed types are observed in humans at specific localizations or whether—as in our case—the composition of the tissue changes over the course of the synovial fold.

question: In a bovine in vitro embryo production study comparing cumulus-oocyte complexes from different follicle sizes, oocytes from large follicles had the poorest recovery and morphology, lower maturation and blastocyst outcomes, increased follicular-fluid malondialdehyde, decreased hypoxanthine, and no matching rise in SOD, GPx, or total antioxidant capacity. Which mechanism most plausibly accounts for their diminished developmental competence?
A: Reduced hypoxanthine would be expected to increase cAMP and strengthen germinal vesicle arrest, while elevated malondialdehyde primarily indicates improved membrane remodeling for fertilization.
B: Elevated malondialdehyde indicates enhanced enzymatic antioxidant defense, and the lack of SOD and GPx increase suggests that oxidative injury is unlikely to contribute to oocyte degeneration.
C: Reduced hypoxanthine may lessen phosphodiesterase inhibition, lowering intra-oocyte cAMP and destabilizing meiotic arrest, while elevated lipid peroxidation with inadequate antioxidant buffering can impair mitochondrial integrity.
D: Poor competence is best attributed to excessive glycolysis and pyruvate metabolism in follicular fluid, which accelerate cytoplasmic maturation beyond nuclear maturation.
Contextual materials: In contrast, although small follicles yielded the highest COC recovery rate (55.11%) and the highest proportion of top-quality oocytes (Grades A + B, 64.22%), their FF exhibits relatively reduced activity in energy metabolism and signaling pathways, including glycolysis, pyruvate metabolism, and CoA biosynthesis. This pattern is in line with our observation that small follicles showed lower maturation (78.48%), cleavage (57.13%), and blastocyst (29.11%) rates than medium follicles, suggesting that limited metabolic support within the FF microenvironment may constrain meiotic progression and early embryonic development despite favorable recovery and morphology. For large follicles, we observed the lowest recovery rate (32.64%), the lowest proportion of Grades A + B oocytes (26.40%), and reduced developmental competence (maturation 71.28%; blastocyst 26.31%), accompanied by an oxidative FF profile (elevated MDA). Elevated MDA indicates enhanced lipid peroxidation and is consistent with the higher proportion of degenerated oocytes observed in the large-follicle group. Metabolomic analysis further revealed reduced hypoxanthine, which may lessen phosphodiesterase inhibition and decrease cAMP levels, thereby destabilizing meiotic arrest and promoting premature meiotic resumption, a mechanism consistent with the poorer competence of large-follicle oocytes in our IVP outcomes. In parallel, the upregulation of glutamine and anethole may represent an adaptive response to oxidative stress: glutamine can support glutathione synthesis and energy metabolism to improve IVM and fertilization, whereas anethole has been reported to modulate redox balance and mitochondrial function. However, despite the increase in MDA, key antioxidant indicators (SOD, GPx, and T-AOC) did not show a compensatory rise, suggesting insufficient antioxidant buffering, which may allow oxidative damage to accumulate and ultimately impair mitochondrial integrity and oocyte developmental competence.

question: Using infrared thermography to assess broilers under heat stress, which pattern best describes how thermoregulation changes with age from younger birds to those approaching market weight?
A: Older broilers show thermoregulatory responses restricted mainly to the comb, wattle, and eye because peripheral vascular development reduces the need for heat exchange through the limbs and tail.
B: Younger broilers show the strongest whole-body thermal recovery because immature cardiovascular control causes generalized vasodilation across all surface regions.
C: Neck and back surface temperatures become less responsive with age because respiratory maturation replaces cutaneous heat exchange as the principal route of thermoregulation.
D: Older broilers exhibit broader and stronger regional thermal responses, including increased involvement of peripheral areas such as the tail and drumstick, consistent with maturation of cardiovascular and integumentary heat-dissipation capacity.
Contextual materials: A key insight from this study is how thermal sensitivity increases with age. Older broilers (35–39 days) exhibit broader and more intense thermoregulatory activity across different body regions, with more areas surpassing the strong-effect threshold $( \boldsymbol { \eta } ^ { 2 } \ge 0 . 1 4 )$ This result reflects the physiological development of the cardiovascular and respiratory systems, which enhances their ability to redistribute heat in response to stress. The increased involvement of peripheral zones, such as the tail and drumstick, in later stages suggests a progressively expanded thermoregulatory network as broilers approach market weight, likely due to increased peripheral vascularization and enhanced blood flow capacity in response to thermal loads. This physiological adaptation enables greater surface area for heat dissipation and aligns with findings that thermoregulation improves with cardiovascular and integumentary maturation in older broilers. Some regions, such as the neck and back, shift from moderate to strong responders with age, indicating developmental changes in vascular control and surface heat exchange. These dynamics highlight the importance of age-specific thermal reference values when using infrared thermography (IRT) in commercial settings. Although the comb, wattle, and eye regions consistently exhibited positive thermal recovery values across all ages, a slight reduction in recovery magnitude was observed in older broilers, which may indicate age-related declines in peripheral vasodilation efficiency or thermal regulatory capacity.

question: In examining the ear region of a European hedgehog skull, which statement accurately identifies the structures involved in the tympanic bulla area and explains why the adjacent cavitylike space is not considered a true tympanic cavity?
A: The petrous part of the temporal bone bears a tympanic process that contributes with the tympanic wing of the basisphenoid to the lesser bony tympanic bulla, while the ectotympanic is an arched plate not ossified with the rest of the skull, so the space it limits is not a true tympanic cavity.
B: The squamous part of the temporal bone forms the bony tympanic bulla with the occipital bone, while the cavitylike space is excluded from the tympanic cavity because it opens through the temporal foramen.
C: The zygomatic process of the temporal bone forms the ectotympanic with the presphenoid, and the enclosed space is not a tympanic cavity because it is occupied by the mandibular fossa.
D: The mastoid process and retroarticular process fuse to form the tympanic bulla, while the cavitylike space is not a tympanic cavity because it is closed laterally by the tympanic process of the basisphenoid.
Contextual materials: Te temporal bone connects caudally to the occipital bone and medially to the presphenoid (os presphenoidale) and basisphenoid bone (os presphenoidale). Two parts of this bone have been identifed in European hedgehogs— the petrosal (pars petrosa), and squamous part (pars squamosa). Te most lateral part of the temporal bone is its’ squamous part. Rostrally, it forms the long zygomatic process of the temporal bone (processus zygomaticus ossis temporalis). On the superior side, it is performed by one or more opening-temporal foramen (foramen temporalis) leading to the temporal canal (canalis temporalis). On the underside of the bone, there is a moderately fat mandibular fossa (fossa mandibularis) with retroarticular foramen (foramen retroarticulare), and a slightly prominent retroarticular process (processus retroarticularis). Tis process links to the mastoid process—a round-shaped process arising for the petrous part of the temporal bone. Behind the basal part of the process lies the petrous part of the temporal bone. Te petrous part has the tympanic process (processus tympanicus) that, along with the tympanic wing of the basisphenoid forms caudolaterally the lesser, the bony part of the tympanic bulla (bulla tympanica) (Fig. 4). Te tympanic bone forms and arched plate not ossifed with the rest to the skull—ectotympanic (tympanum). Te ectotympanic limits the cavitylike space, though it cannot be called a tympanic cavity (cavum tympanicum), since the whole structure is not ossifed. Tis space is closed from the medial aspect by a tympanic process of the basisphenoid.

question: In a dairy heifer showing ambiguous external genitalia and increased anovulval distance, freemartinism was first suspected. Necropsy reveals a blind-ending vagina and a caudally prolonged urethra within erectile-type tissue, with bulbospongiosus and retractor penis muscles present but no glans penis or prepuce. What anatomical interpretation is most consistent with these observations?
A: Typical freemartinism characterized only by Müllerian duct regression, with no evidence of masculinized external genital structures.
B: A shortened rudimentary penis-like structure associated with an extended urethra, lacking a glans and prepuce but accompanied by male-type perineal musculature.
C: A persistent urogenital sinus with a normal female vestibule and intact cervix, explaining the increased anovulval distance.
D: Isolated clitoral hypertrophy without involvement of the urethra or development of penile-associated muscles.
Contextual materials: Ambiguous external genitalia, such as an enlarged clitoris, increased anovulval distance, and the presence of long vulval hair, are occasionally observed in freemartins, while abnormal development of the internal genital tract (short vagina, absence of cervix, hypoplastic uterus) are common in such animals. An increased anovulval distance was seen in the DSD heifer presented here. Our preliminary assumption was thus that this animal represented a case of freemartinism. However, postmortem anatomical and histological studies revealed other abnormalities, including a blind vagina and an extended urethra surrounded by tissues typical of a rudimentary penis. The resulting structure can be considered a shortened penis lacking the glans and prepuce. However, it was accompanied by a bulbospongiosus muscle and penile retractor muscle.

question: Which description most accurately differentiates the cervical esophagus, crop, and thoracic esophagus of a chicken, including the mucosal fold patterns in these regions?
A: The cervical esophagus remains dorsal to the trachea in the midline throughout the neck, the crop lies deep to the breast muscles, and both cervical and crop mucosa show fine longitudinal folds.
B: The crop arises from the thoracic esophagus caudal to the syrinx, lies within the thoracoabdominal cavity cranial to the proventriculus, and has fine longitudinal folds continuous with those of the thoracic esophagus.
C: The cervical esophagus extends from the pharyngo-esophageal junction to the thoracic inlet and shifts to the right ventrolateral neck, the crop is a subcutaneous spindle-shaped expansion anterior to the breast muscles, and the thoracic esophagus lies dorsal to the trachea and syrinx with fine longitudinal mucosal folds.
D: The thoracic esophagus begins at the pharynx, passes ventral to the larynx, forms a left-sided cervical crop, and enters the gizzard without an intervening proventriculus.
Contextual materials: The esophagus of the Gasgie chicken was identified as a long, muscular tube extending from the pharynx to the proventriculus and anatomically divided into cervical, crop, and thoracic regions. The cervical portion extended from the pharyngo-esophageal junction to the thoracic inlet, where it expanded to form the crop. Initially, the cervical esophagus was positioned along the midline dorsal to the larynx and trachea but became laterally displaced in the middle cervical region, lying on the right ventro-lateral aspect (Fig. 2). The crop originated from the cervical esophagus at the thoracic inlet and exhibited a gentle spindle shape with a slight bulge. It was located subcutaneously, anterior to the breast muscles. The thoracic esophagus was located within the thoracoabdominal cavity, dorsal to the trachea and syrinx, and cranial to the proventriculus. Fine longitudinal mucosa folds were consistently observed in the cervical and thoracic regions, while the crop showed irregularly arranged folds (Fig. 3).

question: In an equine hindbrain and cerebellar arterial dissection, a vessel branches from the caudal cerebellar artery and runs laterally with the vestibulocochlear nerve toward the internal auditory meatus. How should this vessel and its main blood supply territory be identified?
A: It is the rostral cerebellar artery, supplying the rostral cerebellar hemispheres.
B: It is the caudal communicating artery, completing the caudal part of the cerebral arterial circle.
C: It is a basilar root of the rostral cerebellar artery, supplying the lateral and caudal cerebellar hemispheres.
D: It is the labyrinthine artery, supplying the inner ear and adjacent choroid plexus.
Contextual materials: After the two basilar segments unite to form the main basilar artery, the basilar artery gives rise to the right and left caudal cerebellar arteries. These arteries course dorsolaterally toward the caudal aspect of the cerebellum, supplying blood to the lateral and caudal portions of the cerebellar hemispheres and the vermis (Figures 1, 2b). The caudal cerebellar artery gave rise to the labyrinthine artery, which coursed laterally toward the internal auditory meatus in association with the vestibulocochlear nerve, supplying the inner ear and the adjacent choroid plexus (Figure 2b). Near the rostral border of the pons, the basilar artery gave rise to three to four roots creating paired rostral cerebellar arteries. These vessels ascended dorsolaterally to supply the rostral cerebellar hemispheres. The basilar artery continued rostrally until joining the caudal communicating arteries, contributing to the cerebral arterial circle (Circle of Willis; Figure 1). Variations occurred in the caliber and branching patterns of the rostral cerebellar arteries in several specimens. Occasional duplication of the initial roots, ranging from three to five, was observed. Minor asymmetries between the left and right caudal cerebellar arteries were present, with one side forming a more dominant trunk in three of the 10 brains examined. In five samples, one or two roots on one or both sides originated from the caudal communicating artery, besides those arising from the basilar artery (Figure 1).

question: In beef calves undergoing postnatal skeletal growth, quantitative bone measurements indicate periosteal expansion without endosteal expansion in the metacarpus, while the humerus expands proportionally at both the periosteal and endosteal surfaces. What is the best interpretation of the biomechanical significance of this humeral growth pattern relative to the metacarpal pattern?
A: The humerus is increasing strength efficiently by expanding both outer and inner circumferences, improving section strength with relatively little added bone mass.
B: The humerus is weakening because proportional endosteal expansion prevents any increase in periosteal diameter or resistance to bending.
C: The humerus is increasing cortical thickness primarily through endosteal infilling, producing greater strength only by substantially increasing bone mass.
D: The humerus is undergoing the same cortical deposition pattern as the metacarpus, indicating that muscular strain has little effect on regional bone adaptation.
Contextual materials: Diferences in the pattern of growth between the metacarpus and humerus were observed that reflected the relative growth of the two bones during the study period and the diferences in mechanical loading of the bones due to bodyweight and muscular strain. Endosteal circumference did not increase in the metacarpal but periosteal circumference increased, demonstrating that cortical bone $( > 7 1 0 \mathrm { m g } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 3 } )$ was being deposited on the outside of the bone resulting in increased cortical thickness, bone area/size and, therefore, bone strength. However, in the humerus, endosteal circumference increased proportionally with periosteal circumference. This appositional growth is a highly eficient mechanism to increase bone strength (SSI) during growth, with minimal increases in bone mass, and thus, only a marginal increase in the resources required for bone growth.

question: Which conclusion best fits a post-weaning calf nutrition study in which feeding a bioactive plant extract containing sanguinarine and chelerythrine increased rumen papillae length but not width, raised villus height-to-crypt depth ratios across several small-intestinal regions, and increased jejunal crypt depth, while showing no consistent intestinal morphology effects of sex, breed, or sex-by-treatment?
A: The extract primarily impaired volatile fatty acid absorption because papillae width, rather than papillae length, is the sole determinant of ruminal absorptive surface area.
B: The extract likely enhanced ruminal and intestinal absorptive morphology, although the increased jejunal crypt depth should be interpreted cautiously because deeper crypts can reflect epithelial inflammation or turnover.
C: The morphologic response was mainly sex-dependent, indicating that male calves should be expected to show improved intestinal barrier function while female calves should not.
D: The extract reduced intestinal barrier function because higher villus height-to-crypt depth ratios indicate greater transfer of digesta-derived toxins into the bloodstream.
Contextual materials: The effects of feeding MCE on rumen papillae and small intestinal morphology are presented in Table 2. In alignment with weaned piglets, TRT increased villus height and villus height: crypt depth in duodenum and ileum $( p < 0 . 0 7 0 )$ , and villus height: crypt depth in the jejunum $( p = 0 . 0 2 2 )$ of the small intestine. Additionally, TRT increased crypt depth in the jejunum compared to CTL $( p = 0 . 0 3 3 )$ . The data did not support an effect of sex $( p = 0 . 2 5 0 )$ , sex × treatment $( p = 0 . 1 3 0 )$ , or breed $( p = 0 . 7 6 0 )$ on any intestinal morphology parameters across the duodenum, jejunum, and ileum. Taller villi represent increased digestive and absorptive capacities, whereas deeper crypts can indicate inflammations in the intestinal epithelium. Moreover, high villus height to crypt depth ratios can be a positive indicator of intestinal barrier function, reducing pathogen and toxin transfer from intestinal digesta to the bloodstream. Feeding MCE also increased papillae length in the rumen $( p = 0 . 0 1 3 )$ , while papillae width remained similar between CTL and TRT suggesting an elevated capacity for VFA absorption. In support, Lima et al. demonstrated an increased surface area of rumen papillae in MCE-fed sheep. The data did not support an effect of sex $( p = 0 . 6 4 9 )$ or sex × treatment $( p = 0 . 1 9 7 )$ on papillae length. The papillae width of male calves was greater than that of female calves (535 vs. 485 mm, $p = 0 . 0 0 2 )$ . Nevertheless, the consistent responses of both rumen papillae and intestinal villi to MCE agreed with Górka et al., demonstrating simultaneous responses of the rumen and small intestine development to nutritional interventions in dairy calves. The improvements in the ruminal and intestinal morphology can be a result of sanguinarine and chelerythrine in MCE that inhibited the programmed cell death of intestinal mucosa of rats and enhanced the recovery from enteritis in broiler chicks. Given the high risk of intestinal damage and the responsiveness of the intestine to dietary bioactive compounds in pre-weaning calves, the improved intestinal morphology observed post-weaning could be a result of a response to MCE pre-weaning. A comprehensive evaluation representing both pre- and post-weaning stages could better explain the effects of MCE on the gut morphology of calves.

question: When updating a small laboratory rodent simulator for oral gavage and endotracheal intubation training, which head and upper aerodigestive tract design would most appropriately address unrealistic anatomy that can make tube insertion artificially easy and impair skill transfer to live animals?
A: A permanently wide-open oral aperture with a smooth continuous pharyngeal channel leading directly into the stomach.
B: A rigid closed jaw with no oral cavity details, paired with a single collapsible tube representing both the trachea and oesophagus.
C: A movable mandible producing realistic mouth opening, with a flexible tongue, incisors, an epiglottis-like laryngeal entry to a ringed trachea, and a separate dorsal oesophagus of realistic diameter.
D: An enlarged oesophageal lumen placed ventral to the trachea to simplify differentiation from the airway during beginner training.
Contextual materials: In the evaluations, the head was the least favorable body part, with a mean score of 4.54. From an anatomical point of view, this needs to be improved dramatically in a novel simulator. Despite reasonable shape and proportions of the head, the evaluators perceived the mobility of the lower jaw and the appearance of the oral cavity as unrealistic. This is problematic, as an anatomically erroneously structured oral cavity would negatively affect the learning processes of challenging techniques, such as oral administration or endotracheal intubation. In addition, these techniques are potentially associated with adverse consequences, such as oesophageal trauma and aspiration pneumonia. Some simulators in this study had wide-open oral openings, which falsely facilitates the insertion of feeding tubes. Consequently, a movable lower jaw that is associated with a realistically opening and closing of the mouth is important. The anatomical appearance would thus be improved by the presence of a flexible tongue as well as upper and lower incisors, comparable in size to those of living rats. A larynx with an epiglottis-like entry should lead to a trachea characterized by semi-solid rings, mimicking normal tracheal cartilages of a live rat. Dorsal to the trachea, a separate oesophagus, with a realistic diameter needs to be implemented.

question: In a beef calf's removed duplicated accessory forelimb, where two left forelimb components share one scapula and one humerus and the distal metacarpals, phalanges, and digital joints are relatively typical, which soft-tissue feature would most accurately describe the malformed extremity?
A: Well-developed intrinsic and extrinsic limb muscles with separate tendinous insertions for each duplicated digit.
B: Complete duplication of the brachial plexus and paired palmar venous drainage accompanying each metacarpal artery.
C: Normal antebrachial musculature but absent metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal articulations due to failure of distal segmentation.
D: Absence of discernible muscle tissue, with tendons largely fused to fascia or periosteum and only rudimentary extensor and flexor tendons identifiable.
Contextual materials: A gross anatomical dissection was performed on the removed accessory limb. The extremity consisted of two left front limbs sharing one common scapula and one common humerus. Further distally, the bones included ossa antebrachii lacking typical characteristics and partially fused ossa carpi. Metacarpal bones and phalanges were typical as well as the metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal articulations. No discernible muscle tissue could be identified, and tendons were firmly combined with fascia or periost. Only rudimentary tendons of the lateral digital extensor muscle and of the deep digital flexor muscle could be distinguished. On the palmar side, two metacarpal arteries and one single vein were recognizable as well as the equivalents of the common digital dorsal artery, vein and nerve.

question: In equine trigeminal cave contrast cisternography with subsequent microCT, where iodinated contrast delineates CSF-containing subarachnoid spaces rather than dense ganglionic neural tissue, how should prominent caudal contrast accumulation with longitudinal filling defects and a trabecular pattern near the porus trigeminus be interpreted when the rostral portion has minimal or absent contrast?
A: The caudal region contains the trigeminal plexus within an expanded subarachnoid space, whereas the rostral low-contrast region corresponds to the denser trigeminal ganglion.
B: The caudal region represents the trigeminal ganglion surrounded by epidural fat, whereas the rostral low-contrast region corresponds to the trigeminal plexus compressed by dura mater.
C: The caudal trabecular contrast pattern indicates intraneural hemorrhage within the trigeminal ganglion, whereas rostral contrast loss indicates free communication with the subdural space.
D: The caudal filling defects represent bony trabeculae of the petrous temporal bone, whereas the rostral low-contrast region indicates contrast leakage into the cavernous sinus.
Contextual materials: In humans, the segments of the trigeminal nerve contained within the trigeminal cave are the trigeminal ganglion and the trigeminal plexus (Figure 1). The subarachnoid space within the trigeminal cave is located posteriorly to the trigeminal ganglion as the arachnoid is thought to tightly adhere to the trigeminal ganglion at its anterior surface (Figure 1). However, a consensus on the meningeal architecture has not yet been reached and three models of the relationship between the meninges and the trigeminal ganglion have been discussed to describe the course and end of the arachnoid membrane and the dura mater around the trigeminal ganglion and its divisions. Based on the distribution of the contrast agent in the subarachnoid space as determined by microCT analysis, it was possible in this study to divide the equine trigeminal nerve into two parts, as observed in humans. The trigeminal ganglion was located rostrally within the trigeminal cave. Upon contrast cisternography and microCT this was characterized by a lack of contrast agent due to its high tissue density, obviously not allowing penetration of the contrast agent. The trigeminal plexus was located within the caudal two thirds of the trigeminal cave near the porus trigeminus and viewed as increased accumulation of contrast agent with longitudinal filling defects and a trabecular pattern. The latter indicated that the trigeminal plexus is located within a widening of the subarachnoid space, comparable to the human trigeminal cistern. In the cistern in horses, the subarachnoid space containing the CSF was not only situated at the periphery of the nerve, but also between the nerve fascicles, i.e., the trigeminal plexus (Figure 1). On MR images, it was equally observed that the fluid arranged in a trabecular pattern between nerve fascicles and the trigeminal ganglion. This explained the trabecular pattern of the distribution of the contrast agent in this region. When the nerve fascicles converged rostrally to form the trigeminal ganglion, the contrast agent column was displaced toward the axial periphery of the trigeminal ganglion, and even disappeared focally (mainly abaxially) due to the adherence of the arachnoid membrane to the ganglionic tissue.

question: When selecting a TAP injection approach for pigs needing abdominal wall analgesia for an incision reaching cranially toward the xiphoid process, how should the findings be interpreted if prior two- and three-point methods reached only about the fifth-last or fourth-last thoracic nerve, whereas a closer-site four-point method more often stained cranial thoracic nerves but stained L2 only inconsistently and did not stain L3?
A: The earlier two-point TAP technique is preferable because staining fewer cranial thoracic nerves indicates more selective blockade of the xiphoid region.
B: The four-point TAP technique is more likely than the earlier techniques to desensitize the cranial abdominal wall, but it may still provide unreliable coverage of the most caudal lumbar nerves.
C: The four-point TAP technique should reliably desensitize L2 and L3 because increasing the number of injection sites primarily promotes caudal lumbar spread.
D: All TAP techniques described would be expected to provide equivalent cranial abdominal wall desensitization because the total number of thoracic vertebrae in pigs is clinically irrelevant.
Contextual materials: Based on the dye distribution with previously described TAP injection techniques in pig cadavers, desensitisation of a sufficient extent of the cranial part of the abdominal wall would not be achieved for surgeries requiring incisions up to the xyphoid process. The most cranial nerve stained with a two- and threepoint TAP technique using 0.3 mL/kg of dye per hemiabdomen was the fifth-last thoracic nerve. Using a two-point TAP technique and 0.3 mL of dye per injection point, the fourth-last thoracic nerve was the most cranial nerve stained. In contrast, with the four-point TAP technique using 0.2 mL/kg of dye per injection point (0.8 mL/kg per hemiabdomen) in this study, the most cranial nerve positively stained was the eighth-last thoracic nerve, although in only one hemiabdomen. The seventh-last thoracic nerve was positively stained in six out of eight hemiabdomens, while the fifth-last thoracic nerve was positively stained in all cases. The injection points were closer together in the four-point TAP technique than in the three-point TAP technique, resulting in more positively stained nerves and the intertwining of certain adjacent dye stains with former technique. Since modern breeds of pigs have 14 to 16 thoracic vertebrae, we believe that a four-point TAP technique could provide better desensitisation of the cranial abdominal wall in pigs compared to the three-point TAP technique. Using the four-point TAP technique, the L2 nerve was stained with little success (3/8), and the L3 nerve was not stained at all. If the volume and concentration of the local anaesthetic allowed for it, a higher volume for the most caudal injection would probably result in a more caudal spread of dye.

question: After saline distension during preparation for equine temporomandibular joint arthroscopy, which observation would best verify entry into the dorsal temporomandibular joint compartment instead of the disc-mandibular compartment?
A: Palpable rostral and lateral distension beneath the intra-articular disc at and below the level of the mandibular condylar process.
B: Dorsal movement of the intra-articular disc when the needle hub is deflected ventrally.
C: Capsular distension dorsal to the intra-articular disc while the caudal contour of the mandible remains anatomically preserved.
D: Fluid reflux into the syringe when plunger pressure is released after compartment distension.
Contextual materials: To prevent fluid extravasation due to the diferences in the size of the arthroscopic cannulae, the joint compartments of the TMJs were first examined using NAS and then STAN. Each TMJ was palpated identifying the intra-articular disc and caudal extent of the condylar process of the mandible. To assess the DTJ a 20G 1 needle was placed directly into the joint compartment in a lateromedial direction immediately dorsal to the intra-articular disc and ventral to the lateral extent of the mandibular fossa of the temporal bone. Access to the DMJ was achieved by placing the 20G 1 needle in either a lateromedial direction, dorsal to the condylar process of the mandible, immediately under the intra-articular disc; or as previously described, into the caudal aspect of the joint from a caudodorsal to the rostroventral direction (when viewed from the side of the horse). Irrespective of needle position, ventral deflection of the hub resulting in dorsal movement of the intra-articular disc was used to confirm placement. Five milliliters of saline were used to distend the joint compartments. DTJ access was confirmed by distention of the joint capsule dorsal to the intra-articular disc with retention of the anatomical contour of the caudal aspect of the mandible. DMJ access was confirmed when the joint compartment at, and below, the palpable level of the condylar process of the mandible occurred. Additionally, rostral and lateral distention of the joint under the intra-articular disc could be palpated. Fluid reflux into the syringe when the plunger pressure was released was another way to confirm correct needle placement into either joint space. Irrespective of the chosen joint compartment, or arthroscope system, a straight Beaver (376700) blade was used to make a vertical skin and capsular incision.

question: When using transverse palmaro-medial ultrasound to identify the palmar digital neurovascular bundle at the horse fetlock, which anatomical-sonographic arrangement should be found?
A: The medial common palmar digital nerve lies deep to the medial palmar digital artery, and both terminal nerve branches remain dorsal to the artery after division.
B: The medial palmar digital vein is typically a thick-walled pulsatile structure positioned palmar to the palmar digital nerve, while the artery is thin-walled and compressible.
C: The ergot vein, when visible, courses dorsal to the medial palmar digital artery and arises independently rather than from the medial palmar digital vein.
D: The medial common palmar digital nerve lies superficial to the medial palmar digital artery before dividing, with the proper palmar digital nerve running palmar to the artery and its dorsal ramus running dorsal to the artery.
Contextual materials: In the phase I, a total of 20 forelimbs from 10 horses were examined, obtaining the evaluation of 20 lateral and 20 medial pasterns, and 20 lateral and 20 medial fetlock regions. The position of the diferent anatomical structures and their relationship with the neurovascular bundles were considered consistent in all the limbs evaluated. Transverse palmaro-lateral and palmaro-medial US images of pastern (Figure 4) and fetlock (Figure 5) regions allowed easy identification of the neurovascular bundle close to the skin surface in all horses. In the pastern region, the neurovascular bundles were superficial to the distal branch of the superficial digital flexor tendon and the deep digital flexor tendon. More deeply, the proximal phalanx, the oblique and the straight sesamoidean ligament were visualized. In the fetlock region, the neurovascular bundles were superficial compared to the third metacarpal bone, the lateral or medial branch of the suspensory ligament and the corresponding proximal sesamoid bone. In both regions, the palmar digital veins (PDVs) showed an anechoic vascular bed with a thin wall easily compressible, whereas the palmar digital arteries (PDAs) were smaller, anechoic, round, pulsatile structures with a thicker wall. In addition, in the transverse palmaro-medial scan of the fetlock, the ergot vein, after branching from the medial PDV, was always visible, palmar to the medial PDN. The PDN was always observed palmar to the PDV both on the medial and lateral sides, with a coarse grainy appearance and a clear distinction from the subcutaneous tissue. In the pastern region, the proper PDNs and their intermediate rami, i.e., the dorsal PDN branch of the middle phalanx, were always identified palmar and dorsal to the PDA, respectively. In the fetlock region, the lateral and medial common PDNs were superficial to the lateral and medial PDAs, before branching into the lateral and medial proper PDNs and their corresponding dorsal rami, i.e., dorsal PDN branch of the proximal phalanx, which were observed running palmar and dorsal to the PDA, respectively.

question: When ultrasound-guided fascial plane injections were used in canine cadavers to stain the dorsal branches of cervical nerves, the C5 intertransversospinalis-plane approach spread widely in both directions but did not reliably stain C2, even with a larger volume. By contrast, an injection centered at C2 consistently stained C2 and C3, often stained C4, and seldom extended to C5. Which anatomical explanation most strongly supports choosing the cranial approach for blocking high cervical segments?
A: The C2-centered injection likely bypasses or avoids the limiting effect of a functional fascial barrier near C2 that may restrict cranial spread from more caudal injections.
B: The C5-centered injection fails primarily because the dorsal branches of C2 and C3 do not course within any fascial plane contiguous with the caudal cervical region.
C: The C2-centered injection works because high cervical dorsal branches are stained only by intraneural spread, whereas caudal cervical branches are stained by interfascial spread.
D: The C5-centered injection is less effective because larger injectate volumes preferentially force solution caudally into the thoracic paravertebral space rather than along cervical fascial planes.
Contextual materials: Recently, Herrera-Linares et al. described the intertransversospinalis plane (ITP) block which, despite the diferent nomenclature, targets an anatomically comparable plane to the MCP. However, their technique performed a more caudal approach (C5) using two diferent volumes; their high volume is equivalent to the one used in the present study. Their results revealed extensive craniocaudal spread with broad staining of the DBCNs; nevertheless, C2 was not stained in all cases, even with higher volumes. In contrast, our approach centered directly at the C2 level resulted in 100% staining of the C2 and C3 segments, with relevant 60% staining at C4, while only reaching 13.33% at C5. This diference in distribution could be attributed not only to the distinct injection site but also to the complex fascial organization of the region. Recent human medicine studies on the deep cervical plane (Cervical Cervicis Plane, CCeP) block have hypothesized the existence of an ‘incomplete functional barrier’ at the C2 level. If an analogous structure exists in dogs within the MCP, it could limit the cranial spread of injectate, thereby justifying the use of a cranial approach to ensure successful blockade of the high cervical segments.

question: When identifying the intergeniculate leaflet in the sheep visual thalamus, where the dorsal lateral geniculate region's layered organization may hide a straightforward band-like border, which histological and immunohistochemical finding best supports this subdivision?
A: A sharply linear, cell-poor band between dorsal and ventral geniculate subdivisions, lacking calcium-binding protein immunoreactivity and resembling the typical rodent pattern.
B: A population of large fusiform neurons seen most clearly in coronal Nissl-stained sections, with calbindin- and calretinin-immunoreactive terminal fields helping define its borders.
C: A broad pregeniculate nuclear mass that cannot be separated from the ventral geniculate nucleus unless vasoactive intestinal peptide staining is used.
D: A cluster of small round neurons embedded in the medial geniculate body, identified primarily by absence of retinally derived terminal fields.
Contextual materials: IGL was first described in rats, and golden hamsters as a well-defined band of cells located between the dorsal and ventral medial geniculate bodies. When comparing rodents and higher mammals, such as primates or sheep (present results), the well-defined straight band between dorsal and ventral subdivisions of the visual thalamus were masked and hidden by the complex laminar organization of the dorsal geniculate bodies. However, in our Nissl-stained sheep sections (Figure 2A), large fusiform neurons, delimiting IGL, were more clearly observed in the coronal plane (Figure 3G). In rodents, nevertheless, its architecture is well defined, but both the localization and limits are dificult to distinguish in some gyrencephalic vertebrate species because primates once had a generic wide pregeniculate nucleus (PGN) included both the ventral geniculate nucleus and IGL. In the visual thalamus of the rock cavy (Kerodon rupestris; rodent), IGL is identified as a well-defined and straight band between dorsal and ventral subdivisions, but in marmosets (primates), this subdivision is masked and hidden by the complex laminar organization of the dorsal part of the LG. Due to its intricate architectonic organization, the primate IGL should be neuroanatomically better defined by using additional neurochemical markers (e.g., VIP immunocytochemistry). However, in the ewe, positive Cb and Cr terminal fields, most likely coming from the retina„ allowed us to trace the borders of this subdivision. In summary, due to its larger fusiform neurons and Cb and Cr immunoreactivity (Figures 5B, C), IGL can be well diferentiated from the remaining visual thalamus in the ewe (Figure 3A).

question: Which feline orbital anatomical feature best justifies choosing a lateral or supratemporal needle path for retrobulbar anesthesia instead of using a frontal approach modeled on human ophthalmic techniques?
A: The feline ocular cone is short and spherical, requiring a perpendicular frontal puncture to achieve intraconal anesthetic spread.
B: The feline orbital cavity completely encloses the globe in bone, making lateral needle insertion more likely to contact the orbital wall.
C: The feline orbit is laterally open, permitting access to an oblong craniocaudally oriented ocular cone while keeping the needle farther from the globe.
D: The feline globe is proportionally smaller than the orbital cavity, eliminating concern for accidental ocular puncture during frontal techniques.
Contextual materials: The retrobulbar block (RB) consists of deposition of a local anesthetic within the ocular cone to produce analgesia, immobilization, and protrusion of the eye in corneal and intraocular surgeries. This locoregional anesthesia technique has been described in several domestic animals. In cats, it was first described in a cadaveric study using the dorsomedial approach with a manually bent spinal needle, and in six sedated experimental cats the year after, showing a lower success rate than using ultrasound guidance to aid the correct needle placement. These studies were based on the study published by Accola in dogs showing that the inferior-temporal palpebral approach was easy to perform and provided complete intraconal coverage without complications. Nevertheless, frontal approaches seem more inspired by the RB technique in humans rather than by the small animal orbital anatomy. In the former, the ocular cone can be easily reached only inserting the needle frontally, while in small animals a laterally open orbital cavity ofers easy access for puncturing an oblong cranial-caudal directed ocular cone. Unlike the frontal techniques, the lateral approach described by Chiavaccini et al. may have the advantage of positioning the needle well far from the eye bulb, reducing the risk of accidental puncture of the ocular bulb. Additionally, the configuration of the orbital cone, including its length and lateral surface, allows for accurate targeting. Although an ultrasound (US)-guided supratemporal technique has been recently mentioned in a cat complicated with suspected brainstem anesthesia, this technique has never been comprehensively described in this species. Some diferences in the needle positioning could be caused by anatomical dissimilarity between dogs and cats, such as a more voluminous ocular globe with the respect of the orbital cavity dimensions in the latter.

question: After pregnant ewes were infected with Shuni virus at gestation day 48 and examined 7 days later, viral RNA testing was performed on plasma, maternal tissues, placentomes, and fetal tissues, with placentome serial sections evaluated by hematoxylin-eosin and viral antigen staining. Which histologic or immunostaining result would most directly indicate early passage of virus across the maternal-fetal interface instead of only maternal viremia?
A: Viral antigen confined to maternal lymph nodes with no antigen detected in placental trophoblasts or fetal tissues.
B: Diffuse maternal fever with plasma viral RNA but absence of viral RNA in placentomes.
C: Hematoxylin-eosin identification of maternal and fetal villi separated by an intact barrier without viral antigen labeling.
D: Viral antigen in maternal placentome epithelium together with antigen in a binucleate trophoblast adjacent to the placental barrier.
Contextual materials: Figure 1. Clinical and laboratory findings following infection of pregnant ewes with Shuni virus (SHUV). (a) Experimental set-up of the pregnant ewe trial. Ewes were inoculated at gestation day (gd) 48. EDTA blood samples were collected and rectal temperatures measured daily. At 7 days post-infection (dpi), the ewes were euthanized and tissue samples collected.rectal temperatures measured daily. At 7 days post-infection (dpi), the ewes were euthanized and tissue samples collected. (b) Rectal temperatures. The moment of inoculation is depicted by the red arrow. (c) Viral RNA in plasma of the ewes and(b) Rectal temperatures. The moment of inoculation is depicted by the red arrow. (c) Viral RNA in plasma of the ewes and (d) (d) viral RNA in maternal organs. Ln: lymph node (e) Viral RNA detected in three placentomes per placenta. Horizontaviral RNA in maternal organs. Ln: lymph node (e) Viral RNA detected in three placentomes per placenta. Horizontal bars bars represent means. (f) Viral RNA detected in fetal organs. (g) Hematoxylin-eosin (HE) staining of a placentome fromrepresent means. (f) Viral RNA detected in fetal organs. (g) Hematoxylin-eosin (HE) staining of a placentome from ewe #197, showing the boundary between a maternal villus (M) and fetal villus (F). Notice the syncytial cell in the maternal epithelium (asterisk). (h) Serial section showing the same area staining for SHUV antigen (visualized by VectorRed). SHUV-positive maternal epithelium is indicted by a blue arrowhead. A single SHUV-positive binucleate trophoblast is indicated by a black arrowhead. Dashed lines mark the placental barrier separating maternal (M) and fetal (F) villi. Bars: 50 µm.

question: When assessing the feline nasal cavity and its bony margins, turbinates, vomeronasal organ, lateral nasal gland, nasal cavernous plexuses, and potential fluid or edema, which statement best describes the respective advantages and limitations of CT, MRI, and rhinoscopy?
A: CT is superior for defining the bony limits of the nasal cavity because bone is hyperattenuating, whereas MRI better differentiates soft tissues and can show fluid or edema as hyperintense on T2-weighted images; rhinoscopy provides direct mucosal visualization but may not reach all caudal structures.
B: MRI is superior for defining cortical bone margins because cortical bone is strongly hyperintense, whereas CT is preferred for identifying the vomeronasal organ and nasal cavernous plexuses; rhinoscopy is generally able to access the entire nasal cavity regardless of specimen condition.
C: Rhinoscopy is the most complete method for mapping both bony and soft-tissue nasal anatomy because it directly visualizes all nasal recesses, whereas CT and MRI are mainly limited to detecting fluid accumulation and cannot reliably distinguish bone from soft tissue.
D: CT and MRI provide equivalent visualization of nasal bone because cortical and medullary bone have identical signal characteristics on MRI; T2-weighted MRI is primarily useful for suppressing edema, while rhinoscopy mainly evaluates structures deep to the mucosa.
Contextual materials: In this study, the advantages and disadvantages of studying the nasal cavity using CT, MRI, and rhinoscopy can be observed. To date, there are no such exhaustive studies of the nasal cavity that encompass both imaging techniques and rhinoscopy. CT allowed the bony limits and extensions of the nasal cavity to be identified much better than with MRI, since, in their entirety, they are completely hyperattenuated. With MRI, the bone was observed with different signal intensities depending on whether it was cortical or medullary, which in many cases makes it difficult to visualize the bone limits. The cortical layer, due to its low concentration of hydrogen atoms, was observed to be hypointense, while the medullary, as it contains bone marrow, which is rich in fat and therefore has a greater amount of hydrogen atoms, was observed to be hyperintense. In contrast, the MRI study provided better detail of the soft tissue, which allowed for clearer observation of the entire development of the turbinates, vomeronasal organ, lateral nasal gland, and nasal cavernous plexuses. Furthermore, with T2-weighted MRI, fluids and edema can be visualized as hyperintense, which can help in the interpretation of pathological conditions. The rhinoscopic study, for its part, allowed for a direct visualization of the nasal cavity; however, it has the limitation that it cannot access all structures due to the restriction that rhinoscope access can pose in many areas. In our study, due to the rigidity after preservation with fixative solution of the leopard’s head, it was impossible to access the more caudal levels. In this context, it is also worth highlighting the different colors of the mucosa of the nasal cavity of the domestic cat compared to the big cats, which was shown to have a much more vivid and pink color in the cat, “as it is a living animal”. This is due to the effect of the fixative solution on the mucosa, since the rhinoscopic study of big cats was performed, unlike in the domestic cat, on fixed specimens.

question: For a dog undergoing guided mandibular ostectomy with an oscillating saw, how should the anatomy-related hemorrhage concern from mandibular neurovascular bundle transection be managed, and what does current evidence indicate about choosing piezosurgery instead?
A: The inferior alveolar artery should be ligated at the mental foramen on the lateral mandible before osteotomy, and current veterinary studies show piezosurgery consistently improves mandibular ostectomy accuracy compared with oscillating saws.
B: Hemorrhage can be minimized by ligating the inferior alveolar artery as it enters the mandibular foramen on the medial mandibular surface, but veterinary evidence is insufficient to conclude that piezosurgery is superior to an oscillating saw for this application.
C: The main vessel at risk is the facial artery where it crosses the ventral mandibular border, so bleeding control is best achieved after guide removal by cauterizing the masseteric surface rather than addressing the mandibular canal contents.
D: Because piezosurgery selectively spares all neurovascular structures during bone cutting, direct isolation or ligation of the inferior alveolar neurovascular bundle is unnecessary when a surgical guide is used.
Contextual materials: In all cases in this study, the neurovascular bundle was sharply transected using an oscillating saw. Soft tissue trauma was documented with respect to injury to the gingiva, surrounding musculature, and other adjacent structures, but not specifically to the neurovascular bundle itself. Clinically, hemorrhage would be managed either pre-osteotomy through ligation of the inferior alveolar artery as it enters the mandibular foramen on the medial aspect of the mandible, or post-osteotomy following removal of the surgical guide. Evaluation of piezotome use in conjunction with surgical guides, including its effects on accuracy and direct comparison with an oscillating saw, would be an interesting direction for future investigation, with the potential added benefit of improved control and precision during isolation and ligation of the neurovascular bundle. While the human medical literature demonstrates benefits of piezosurgery compared with oscillating saws, such evidence is currently lacking in the veterinary literature. As a result, ostectomy device choice remains dependent on surgeon preference and institutional practice.

question: After estradiol-17β stimulation in rabbit uterine epithelium, time-series transcriptomics found up-regulated JAK–STAT and TNF signaling in the luminal epithelium, up-regulated retinol metabolism in the glandular epithelium, and down-regulated sphingolipid metabolism in both compartments. Which option best explains how these pathway shifts relate to embryo implantation mechanisms?
A: Luminal epithelial TNF signaling primarily suppresses NF-κB and MAPK activity to prevent inflammatory tolerance, while glandular retinol metabolism mainly generates sphingomyelin to stabilize trophoblast membranes during early attachment.
B: Glandular epithelial JAK–STAT activation is the principal marker of estradiol-induced receptivity, whereas luminal epithelial retinol metabolism down-regulation indicates reduced retinoic acid production and inhibition of epithelial differentiation.
C: Luminal epithelial JAK–STAT activation may promote receptivity through LIF-STAT3 signaling, TNF signaling may modulate attachment-related inflammatory and immune responses through MAPK/NF-κB pathways, and glandular retinol metabolism may influence differentiation through retinoic acid-dependent nuclear receptor signaling.
D: Reduced sphingolipid metabolism in both epithelial compartments indicates enhanced branched-chain amino acid catabolism, which directly supplies valine, leucine, and isoleucine for retinoic acid synthesis during implantation.
Contextual materials: Time-series clustering using Mfuzz revealed dynamic, compartmentspecific transcriptional programs in the LE and GE in response to estradiol-17β stimulation. Notably, three distinct gene expression trajectories were identified in each epithelial subtype, highlighting temporally coordinated shifts in signaling and metabolic activity. Our results showed that the JAK–STAT and TNF signaling pathways were significantly up-regulated in the LE, indicating the JAK–STAT pathway plays an important role in embryo implantation, and these are consistent with the existing studies, activation of STAT3 through LIF, which regulates the receptivity of the uterine epithelium and embryo implantation. TNF-α regulates the inflammatory response, apoptosis, and immune tolerance of the endometrium through the activation of the MAPK and NF-κB pathways, which in turn afects the embryo’s attachment to the uterus. The results also showed that sphingolipid metabolism was significantly down-regulated in GE and LE. It has been shown that sphingolipid metabolism regulates cell membrane structure and signaling during embryo implantation, particularly through sphingolipid molecules (e.g., sphingomyelin), which regulate cell proliferation and apoptosis. It is shown that this pathway plays an important role in the later stages of embryo implantation. Sphingolipid metabolism has been shown to play an important role in uterine epithelial receptivity and embryo attachment. Retinol metabolism is significantly up-regulated in the GE in our study. Retinol metabolism regulates cell diferentiation and development during embryo implantation, particularly through retinoic acid (RA), which in turn regulates gene expression. Retinol is metabolized to produce RA, which regulates gene expression by binding to nuclear receptors, which in turn afects embryonic development and cell diferentiation. Our time-series analysis also suggested that the valine, leucine, and isoleucine degradation pathway was decreased in the LE and GE. Future studies can further explore the efects of valine, leucine, and isoleucine degradation on embryo implantation. Furthermore, GE-specific upregulation of AGE-RAGE signaling and microRNAs in cancer suggests that GE undergoes distinct stress-related or epigenetic modulation during the receptive window, a topic warranting further investigation.

question: When female ducks nearing first oviposition are monitored over the last weeks before the first egg and just after laying, with cloacal morphology scored from class 1 to class 4, which interpretation best separates a practical pre-laying sign from a finding that mainly confirms laying afterward?
A: Class 1 morphology is the most useful indicator of imminent oviposition because it remains dominant until 2–3 days before the first egg and then increases after laying.
B: Class 4 morphology is the earliest reliable pre-laying indicator because nearly all ducks show it 25–26 days before the first egg and it disappears after laying.
C: Class 3 morphology is mainly a post-laying confirmation sign because it is rare before the first egg but appears in nearly all ducks only after oviposition.
D: Class 3 morphology is a strong indicator of imminent first oviposition because it becomes very common 2–3 days before the first egg, whereas class 4 is uncommon before laying but predominates after the egg is laid.
Contextual materials: The results demonstrated in Table 3 indicate that significant alterations in the cloaca’s morphology were visible as early as on the 25th or 26th day before the start of laying. Every female duck showed a class 1 morphology. After the 25th and 26th day before laying, 75% of the ducks were still classified as class 1. The proportion of animals with class 3 cloacae significantly increased prior to the first or second day before egg-laying $( p = 0 . 0 0 3 )$ . Up until the 9th or 10th day before the first egg, the number of class 1 cloacae drastically decreased $( p < 0 . 0 0 1 )$ . Most animals (97%) demonstrated signs of a class 3 cloaca two-to-three days before their first egg-laying. Prior to egg-laying, only 13% of the ducks showed a class 4 cloaca, whereas, following the laying process, 97% demonstrated a class 4 cloaca. The increase in class 4 cloacae on the third day before egg-laying was deemed statistically significant $( p < 0 . 0 0 1 )$

question: When applying human-developed biportal endoscopic spinal surgery (BESS) to canine disc procedures, which factor best justifies the need for a standardized dog-specific method instead of directly using the human approach?
A: Canine vertebral anatomy and back morphology differ substantially from humans, and BESS requires a precise two-portal triangular approach with specialized instruments.
B: BESS uses a single midline portal and standard arthroscopic instruments, so the main limitation in dogs is the absence of a naturally flat operative surface.
C: Dogs have larger vertebral bodies and flatter backs than humans, making the human BESS portal geometry excessively shallow for safe disc access.
D: The primary barrier is that canine facet joints are absent in the thoracolumbar spine, preventing the use of oblique approaches to the disc space.
Contextual materials: BESS involves two portals obliquely approaching the disc area, creating a precise triangular configuration. This technique and its indications were based on anatomical standards. Significant anatomical differences exist between humans and dogs in vertebral body size and shape, facet joint configuration, spinal canal shape, transverse process position, and angle and extent of the pedicles and lamina. Back morphology also differs: broad and flat in humans, but more rounded in dogs, which complicates the direct adaptation of human techniques in veterinary surgery. In addition, BESS requires specialized instruments beyond those used in the UESS. Collectively, these anatomical and technical differences highlight the need for a standardized methodological framework to safely and reproducibly adapt BESS in dogs.

question: What is the best interpretation of a sow reproductive tract pattern in which mucosal folds are small and sparse at the uterotubal junction but progressively enlarge and occupy more of the lumen toward the ampulla, considering its likely reproductive significance?
A: The ampullary increase in fold size reduces epithelial surface area, limiting contact with ciliated cells and slowing embryo transport during the luteal phase.
B: The progressive increase in oviductal fold size toward the ampulla increases epithelial surface area and may facilitate oocyte or embryo interaction with ciliated cells and fluid-pressure modulation during transport.
C: The sparse folds at the uterotubal junction indicate that this region is the principal site of fertilization because reduced luminal occupancy maximizes sperm-oocyte contact.
D: The maximal fold development during the follicular phase is best explained by predominance of secretory cells, which replace ciliated cells and mechanically propel embryos toward the uterus.
Contextual materials: Like what has been observed in humans or sheep, our results show throughout all phases of the cycle, at the UTJ level, mucosal folds are sparse and smaller in size, occupying limited space within the lumen. However, as we move away from the uterus and progress toward the oviduct until the ampulla, a significant increase in the size of these folds and the proportion of space they occupy within the lumen becomes evident. This increase in lumen occupancy is not only apparent from the measurements of the folds in the images but is also corroborated by the decrease in lacunarity. In addition, even though our sample size is small, it is worth noting that the maximum fold amplitude is consistently observed during the follicular phase, as previously described using electronic microscopy. Cyclic variations during the estrous cycle have been even described in the serosal part of the oviduct where cells of the tubal epithelium are also present, being the ciliated cells predominant during the follicular phase and the secretory cells during the luteal phase. It has been suggested that the folds in the oviduct could play a crucial role in the transport of oocytes and embryos during the fertilization process. These oviductal epithelial folds serve to significantly increase the surface area of the epithelium, thereby enhancing the likelihood of contact between the oocyte/embryo and the ciliated cells within the oviduct. Moreover, the specific structure of these folds appears to play a key role in alleviating the pressure diference in the oviductal fluid before and after the passage of the oocyte/embryo. It has been observed that the Celsr1 gene controls the proper formation of these oviductal folds, and Celsr1-deficient mice present an altered ciliary beating coordination, and aberrant fold orientation distribution, even leading to infertility, presumably due to dificulties in the efective transport of oocytes and embryos through the oviduct.

question: For MR-based volumetric assessment of the feline hippocampal formation, how should investigators handle the unclear macroscopic and imaging boundary between the subicular complex and parahippocampal gyrus to maintain comparability across studies?
A: Exclude the subicular complex entirely because its transition to the parahippocampal gyrus is always identifiable only on T2-weighted MR images.
B: Define the boundary by cerebrospinal fluid signal because the normal feline ventricular system reliably outlines the rostromedial hippocampal margin.
C: Use a reproducible geometric boundary anchored to clearly visible cortical landmarks, recognizing it as an approximate rather than exact histologic delineation.
D: Rely primarily on visualization of the alveus in routine clinical MR planes because it remains conspicuous independent of image resolution or orientation.
Contextual materials: There are several definitions of the boundaries of the HF. In veterinarian medicine, the delineation of the HF is mostly described as being done through the CSF and the alveus in the rostromedial and lateral parts of the HF. Delineation with the aid of the CSF, even in high resolution MR imaging, is rarely possible and this can also be seen in the results from our study, because in the ventricular system of healthy cats it is very small (Figure 1A). Furthermore, delineation of the alveus is dificult and only possible in high resolution MR images; in the opinion of some authors, the alveus is most evident in the planes perpendicular to the long axis of the HF in dogs. The boundaries of the HF were mostly visible in the formalin fixed slices, except from the areas where the hippocampus proper exchanges into the subicular complex and then exchanges into the parahippocampal gyrus (Figure 1A). These boundaries have been insuficiently defined until now, especially for companion animals and using MR imaging, but it is not possible to find a macroscopically clear delineation of these structures (Figures 1C,D). Moreover, the delineation of the anteroventral part of the HF from the amygdala is not fully clear. The lateral caudal borders of the HF could be dificult to distinguish because of the adjacent thalamus. These problems are reinforced in the MR images. Though there is a good white-gray matter contrast in the T2-weighted MR images, the cell structure is even less visible (Figures 1C,D). Some authors who made volumetric measurements of the HF tried to make their results reproducible by defining a line fixed on anatomical structures that are clearly visible for the boundary of the subicular complex to the parahippocampal gyrus. Mu et al. defined the boundary between the subiculum and parahippocampal gyrus by a line in continuation with the inferior border of the subiculum (Figures 3A–D). Milne et al. defined the boundary between the same structures in the oblique dorsal plane as a line perpendicular to the tangent of the cortex at the apex of the cortex as it curved caudomedially. Gardini et al. tried to quantify the HF via linear measurements and by creating a ratio between the height of the brain and the HF height. These methods seem to be a better solution to define a rough boundary and to obtain comparable results for the volumetric measurement (Figures 3A–D). However, for exact delineation, further histological and anatomical investigations are necessary.

question: When a dairy farm changes from Bos cattle to water buffalo, milk flow is slow after the milking cluster is attached under cow-optimized vacuum settings and stimulation routines. Which anatomofunctional factor most directly explains why machine-milking management must be adjusted for water buffalo?
A: A shorter teat canal with a weak sphincter predisposes to passive cisternal drainage, while most milk is stored in the gland cistern and requires minimal neuroendocrine stimulation.
B: A wider teat canal and reduced sphincter tone require lower vacuum levels, while dominant cisternal storage explains delayed milk removal despite immediate oxytocin release.
C: A larger udder with expanded teat cisterns causes excessive residual milk, while reduced alveolar storage makes prestimulation less relevant than pulsation frequency.
D: A longer, narrower teat canal with a thicker sphincter increases outflow resistance, while a high proportion of milk stored in alveoli makes prolonged prestimulation important for milk ejection.
Contextual materials: Abstract: The present review aims to analyze the anatomical and physiological characteristics of the mammary gland and udders of water buffalo by making an anatomofunctional comparison with dairy cattle. It will also discuss the knowledge generated around the physiological regulation of milk ejection in the water buffalo. It was found that buffalo’s average udder depth and width is approximately 20 cm smaller than Bos cattle. One of the main differences with dairy cattle is a longer teat canal length (around 8.25–11.56 cm), which highly influences buffalo milking. In this sense, a narrower teat canal (2.71 ± 0.10 cm) and thicker sphincter muscle are associated with needing higher vacuum levels when using machine milking in buffalo. Moreover, the predominant alveolar fraction of water buffalo storing 90–95% of the entire milk production is another element that can be related to the lower milk yields in buffalo (when compared to Bos cattle) and the requirements for prolonged prestimulation in this species. Considering the anatomical characteristics of water buffalo’s udder could help improve bubaline dairy systems.

question: When tracing the radial nerve and collateral radial artery around the triceps brachii heads in the goat brachium, which arrangement matches the observed pattern that contrasts with the traditional ruminant account?
A: The radial nerve continuation and primary branches to the lateral head and anconeus pass between the medial and accessory heads, while the collateral radial artery usually courses between the accessory and long heads.
B: The radial nerve and collateral radial artery consistently pass laterally between the long and medial heads, with all triceps muscular branches arising distal to this interval.
C: The radial nerve passes between the accessory and lateral heads with branches to the long head arising in the same interval, while the collateral radial artery follows the medial head exclusively.
D: The radial nerve passes through fibers of the accessory head near its origin in most limbs, while the collateral radial artery accompanies branches to the tensor fasciae antebrachii between the medial and long heads.
Contextual materials: Notably, contrary to classical descriptions stating that in ruminants the radial nerve, together with the distal branch of the caudal circumflex humeral artery (collateral radial artery), passes laterally between the long and medial heads of the triceps brachii, dissections in the present study showed that the primary branches to the lateral head and anconeus muscle, along with the continuation of the radial nerve, passed between the medial and accessory heads, while branches to the long head and tensor fasciae antebrachii did not. The precise branching pattern of these muscular nerves has not been described previously in ruminants, although the general course of the radial nerve is consistent with previously reported descriptions in these species. In most carnivorans, the radial nerve passes from the medial to the lateral side of the brachium either between the medial and accessory heads or between the medial and long heads. Additionally, the collateral radial artery coursed between the accessory and long heads in most antimeres, except for three antimeres in which it passed through fibers of the accessory head near its origin. Comparative data from carnivorans further indicate variability: In Canis lupus familiaris, the collateral radial artery passes between the medial and accessory heads. In Cerdocyon thous, it may pass either between the medial and accessory heads or between the accessory and lateral heads. In Procyon cancrivorus and Potos flavus, it runs between the accessory and lateral heads.

question: Given that examined jellynose fishes (Ateleopodiformes) and ctenosquamates such as myctophiforms and acanthomorphs possess a Brockmann body, whereas examined aulopiforms lack this discrete pancreatic endocrine structure, which phylogenetic conclusion follows most directly from a parsimonious interpretation of this character distribution?
A: The Brockmann body is best interpreted as an ancestral teleost character that was independently retained in Aulopiformes and lost in Ateleopodiformes.
B: The Brockmann body is best interpreted as a derived character uniting Ateleopodiformes with Ctenosquamata, excluding Aulopiformes from that neoteleost subgroup.
C: The absence of a Brockmann body is best interpreted as a synapomorphy linking Ateleopodiformes with Aulopiformes to the exclusion of Ctenosquamata.
D: The presence of a Brockmann body is best interpreted as evidence that Stomiiformes and Osmeriformes are nested within Ateleopodiformes.
Contextual materials: Jellynose fshes constitute the small fsh order Ateleopodiformes, with about 12 species in the single family Ateleopodidae. Te phylogenetic placement of this enigmatic fsh order has been the subject of considerable debate among either morphology- or molecule-based studies. Based on morphology, Olney et al. concluded that it forms an unresolved trichotomy with the stomiiforms and eurypterigians (Aulopiformes plus Ctenosquamata). While molecular studies revealed the sister-group relationship between the Stomiiformes and Osmeriformes, the sister group of the Ateleopodiformes remained unresolved (Fig. 3). Our dissections show that a BB is present in two species of the Ateleopodiformes, but is absent in the aulopiform species (Figs. 1 and 2A; Supplementary Table 1). Based on its distribution across teleost fsh taxa, we consider its presence as a synapomorphy of the fshes comprising Ateleopdiformes and Ctenosquamata (Myctophiformes plus Acanthomorpha), or in other words, the Neoteleostei exclusive of the Aulopiformes (Fig. 3). Epple and Brinn already proposed that the presence of a BB is a synapomorphy of the Ctenosquamata. Yet, this hypothesis was weakly supported as the authors examined only few ctenosquamat representatives, lacked data on myctophids, and included only fve acanthomorph genera (Gadus, Lophius, Fundulus, Xiphophorus, and Tilapia). Moreover, they followed the classification proposed by Rosen, where gadids and lophiids were members of the Paracanthopterygii and excluded from the Acanthomorpha. In spite of that, Epple and Brinn’s work remains pioneering in understanding the distribution of pancreatic character-states in vertebrates, especially in ray-fnned fshes. In the present study, we aim to reconsider previously published anatomical data, concomitant with our own observations in the light of molecule-based phylogenies. We support the suggested hypothesis from Epple and Brinn that the presence of a BB is a putative synapomorphy of the Ctenosquamata plus Ateleopodiformes.

question: As pregnancy progresses in ewes, placentome diameter and circulating ovine placental lactogen (oPL) both rise, yet a longitudinal study shows no significant early-gestation correlation between them and brief inverse correlations near mid-gestation. What is the best interpretation of this finding?
