B: Bonamia ostreae: highest protozoan survival and prevalence during sustained temperatures above 25°C combined with low-salinity conditions.
C: Marteilia refringens: sporulation and transmission expected primarily below about 7°C, explaining detections concentrated in winter and spring.
D: Bonamia exitiosa: disease dynamics unaffected by temperature extremes but suppressed by elevated salinity in marine bivalve hosts.
Contextual materials: In the present study, field environmental data, including water temperature, salinity, dissolved oxygen, pH, and chlorophyll-a, were not collected at the time of sampling. This limited our ability to directly evaluate how environmental variability may have influenced the detection of the target parasites. This limitation should be considered when interpreting the present findings. In marine bivalves, the establishment, proliferation, transmission, and clinical expression of parasitic infections can be strongly influenced not only by host susceptibility, but also by water temperature, salinity, seasonality, and host physiological condition. Both P. marinus and P. olseni have been reported to show increased infection intensity and prevalence under relatively high-temperature and high-salinity conditions, particularly above $2 5 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ and 20 PSU. In contrast, B. ostreae is often reported at higher prevalence from winter to spring, and parasitic protozoan stages have been shown to have reduced survival at temperatures above $2 5 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ and under low-salinity conditions. For B. exitiosa, extreme temperatures, particularly below $7 ^ { \circ } C$ or above ${ 2 6 } ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,$ as well as elevated salinity, have been suggested to influence disease dynamics. In the case of M. refringens, a threshold temperature of approximately $1 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ has been proposed for sporulation and transmission, and detections of M. refringens have been reported more frequently during summer and autumn than during winter and spring. Differences in infection intensity and prevalence under these environmental conditions would allow pathogen detection data to be interpreted beyond simple positive or negative results and would help identify environmental conditions and seasonal windows associated with elevated infection risk. Furthermore, evaluating the relationship between environmental variability and pathogen occurrence through long-term, seasonally structured monitoring could contribute to the development of early surveillance and risk prediction frameworks for non-native or regulated parasitic pathogens in Korean aquaculture areas.

question: In a pig herd evaluation of garlic and wormwood preparations for Cryptosporidium spp., infection is found only in sows and weaners rather than neonatal piglets, and treatment produces modest decreases in prevalence and oocyst shedding despite limited quantitative sensitivity of routine coproparasitological methods. Which conclusion best accounts for why these favorable findings may have limited practical clinical value for controlling porcine cryptosporidiosis?
A: Because garlic and wormwood are expected to eliminate Cryptosporidium only when administered to adult boars, treatment of sows and weaners cannot affect environmental contamination.
B: Because Cryptosporidium spp. in pigs is primarily a clinical disease of neonatal piglets, reductions in carrier status among weaners and sows may not translate into a major direct therapeutic benefit in the clinically affected age group.
C: Because Cryptosporidium oocysts are reliably quantified by standard flotation methods, any observed reduction in prevalence necessarily proves complete elimination of infection from the herd.
D: Because Cryptosporidium infections in sows and weaners are usually cytopathic viral coinfections, botanical treatments would be expected to worsen clinical signs in neonatal pigs.
Contextual materials: Cryptosporidiosis is an emerging zoonotic protozoan parasite that poses a global challenge in both veterinary and human medicine. Te fndings revealed its existence, while the usual coproparasitological tehniques lacked the ability to detect the average intensity, due to the absence of quantitative sensitivity in oocyst counting. In the present study, Cryptosporidium spp. was only identifed in weaners and sows, which were considered to serve as a permanent source of infection. Both plants exhibited limited efcacy against Cryptosporidium, causing a decrease in prevalence (Fig. 1 and Fig. 3). In Cryptosporidium infected mice, treatment with raw garlic juice (50 mg/kg, for seven days) also reduced shedding of Cryptosporidium oocysts. In humans, therapy with allicin against Cryptosporidium parvum and Cryptosporidium hominis was successful, indicating a lethal efect on Cryptosporidium, while improving patient immune function. Gaafar et al. performed an in vivo experiment, administering aqueous garlic extract on immunosuppressed mice, and observed a destruction of Cryptosporidium oocysts. Te use of artemisin against C. parvum infection showed limited efectiveness, causing a minor decrease in average oocyst numbers, when compared to macrolides, similar to the results obtained in the present study in pigs. Artemisia ethanolic extracts were used as a remedy in mouse cryptosporidiosis and the results revealed signifcantly reduced oocyst shedding, while the symptoms disappeared in the treated groups. A. absinthium essential oil (2 mg/ml) was able to destroy Cryptosporidium baileyi and Cryptosporidium galli oocysts, in vitro. Considering that the selected age groups were only carriers of the parasite, the practical importance of the efect of garlic and wormwood on cryptosporidiosis might be limited. Cryptosporidium clinically afects only piglets during neonatal period. Terefore, the positive results obtained by both plants, might not have a signifcant impact in this frame.

question: For a layer flock diagnosed with both coccidiosis and Ascaridia galli, which treatment regimen is the appropriate choice rather than those used for broiler flocks or infections that also involve cestodes?
A: Amprolium-Plus in feed and water for 4 days plus fenbendazole in water.
B: Fenbendazole treatment combined with complete litter change.
C: Diclazuril combined with piperazine citrate.
D: Albendazole administered for 1 month.
Contextual materials: In the current study, the following treatments were suggested for mixed parasite infections: 1) the use of albendazole for 1 mo on an egg laying farm with coinfection with A. galli and cestodes, 2) amprolium-Plus in feed and water for 4 consecutive days with a combination of fenbendazole in water in broiler farms with coccidia and A. galli, 3) farms positive for mixed cestodes and A. galli treatment with fenbendazole and litter change is recommended, and 4) amprolium-Plus in feed and piperazine citrate in water, along with a change of litter, are recommended for farms that test positive for coccidia, cestode, and A. galli. In addition, diclazuril with piperazine citrate can be utilized in layer farms with coccidia and A. gallli.

question: In an outdoor winter pig study, groups introduced during an exceptionally cold February showed falling fecal egg or oocyst counts for Oesophagostomum spp. and Eimeria spp., while accumulated Ascaris suum egg counts lacked a similar weather-related decrease. What interpretation most accurately accounts for this difference among parasites?
A: Oesophagostomum and Eimeria transmission increased because cold temperatures accelerate larval migration and oocyst sporulation, whereas A. suum transmission declined because embryonated eggs cannot tolerate any freezing exposure.
B: A. suum egg counts remained stable because pigs acquire immediate sterile immunity after ingestion of unembryonated eggs, whereas Oesophagostomum and Eimeria declined primarily because their adult stages cannot survive in the porcine intestine during winter.
C: The decline in Oesophagostomum and Eimeria was most consistent with reduced fecal output in cold weather, while A. suum was unaffected because its eggs sporulate intracellularly before being shed.
D: Oesophagostomum eggs and free-living larvae and Eimeria oocyst sporulation are relatively vulnerable to freezing or freeze-thaw exposure, whereas A. suum eggs are environmentally resistant and low paddock temperatures likely prevented embryonation of newly excreted eggs.
Contextual materials: The general declining incidence levels observed for Oesophagostomum spp. and Eimeria spp. from SUB1 to SUB4 during winter are most likely due to weather conditions since SUB3 and SUB4 were introduced in February 2021 (3rd and 17th), which was the coldest month recorded during this study. Eggs and free-living larvae of Oesophagostomum spp. are considered very susceptible to extreme weather conditions. A reduction in sporulation has been reported for the porcine E. debliecki and E. scabra exposed to freezing, thawing, and continuous freezing. Moreover, freezing has been found to inactivate chicken Eimeria spp. and reduce bovine Eimeria spp. oocysts when kept at −18◦C. In contrast, the transmission of A. suum appeared unafected by weather conditions during this study, as judged by accumulated FEC over the sub-studies. A. suum eggs are very resistant to environmental conditions, especially when unembryonated, and can survive freezing temperatures down to −27◦C for 10 days when containing embryos, although freezing usually diminishes infectivity. Due to low temperatures during the study, it is unlikely that any embryonation of excreted eggs took place in the paddocks.

question: In dairy cattle given the same dose of meloxicam, postpartum cows show roughly half the systemic clearance and nearly double the systemic exposure seen in mid-lactation cows after either intravenous or oral dosing. Because meloxicam is cleared mainly by hepatic elimination, has little unchanged renal excretion, and exhibits a very low hepatic extraction ratio, which explanation under the well-stirred hepatic clearance model best accounts for hepatic blood flow changes being an unlikely primary driver of this pharmacokinetic difference?
A: For low-extraction drugs, hepatic clearance is governed mainly by unbound fraction and intrinsic metabolic clearance rather than hepatic blood flow.
B: For low-extraction drugs, systemic exposure is determined mainly by renal filtration of unchanged drug rather than hepatic metabolism.
C: For low-extraction drugs, oral bioavailability must be low, so postpartum cows have greater exposure because gastrointestinal absorption is incomplete in mid-lactation cows.
D: For low-extraction drugs, clearance rises proportionally with hepatic blood flow, so reduced postpartum blood flow directly doubles systemic exposure.
Contextual materials: Our group has previously noted that meloxicam persisted at higher concentrations in the plasma for longer in post-partum vs. mid-lactation dairy cattle following oral administration. This finding was confirmed in the current study. In our previous work, we hypothesized that the diference was due to an increased bioavailability of the drug in post-partum cows. To test this hypothesis, the current study was designed to compare the pharmacokinetics of meloxicam between these two groups following both intravenous and oral administration. The results indicated a lower clearance in post-partum vs. mid-lactation cows, independent of the mode of administration, resulting in a longer estimated terminal half-life and increased systemic exposure in post-partum cows. The bioavailability determined in this study is consistent with the literature showing that meloxicam is extensively absorbed after oral dosing. The diference in bioavailability between treatment groups are due to absolute clearance diferences between post-partum and midlactation cows. The clearance in post-partum was approximately half compared to mid-lactation cows. Accordingly, the systemic exposure to meloxicam in post-partum cows was doubled. Meloxicam is a low-extraction ratio drug $\left( E < 0 . 3 \right)$ and, like many other NSAIDs, is primarily eliminated by the liver. Less than 5% of unchanged drug is excreted through the renal system. The results displayed a global extraction ratio of meloxicam for intravenous administration as 0.008 (0.006–0.01) and 0.004 (0.003–0.006) for mid-lactation and post-partum treatment groups, respectively. These results confirm that meloxicam is a low extraction ratio drug in both post-partum and mid-lactation conditions. Extraction ratio for meloxicam has been previously reported in guinea pigs, as 0.0087, which is consistent with the mid-lactation treatment group. Though there is a substantial diference in the hepatic blood flow between post-partum and mid-lactation cows, under the assumptions made by the Well-Stirred model of hepatic drug clearance, changes in blood flow have little impact on clearance of low-extraction ratio drug. The Well-Stirred model can be reduced to two factors that can influence hepatic clearance of meloxicam under the assumption of a low extraction ratio drug. The first being the unbound fraction or free fraction and alternatively, the intrinsic clearance could be decreased. Therefore, clearance of drugs that have a low extraction ratio are determined by the following equation:

question: When ecologically matched forest sites with and without year-round supplemental feeding for white-tailed deer are compared, mean parasite burdens in individual deer and raccoon fecal samples are similar, but fed sites contain far more fecal piles and much higher total environmental nematode and coccidia counts. What is the best interpretation of the elevated transmission risk at the fed sites?
A: Supplemental feeding primarily increases transmission risk by intensifying parasite burdens within each infected host, even when host aggregation is unchanged.
B: Supplemental feeding increases transmission risk by concentrating animals and fecal deposition, thereby raising environmental parasite load despite unchanged per-sample parasite intensity.
C: Supplemental feeding reduces environmental parasite contamination per host, but increases clinical disease by suppressing mucosal immunity in deer.
D: Supplemental feeding increases only protozoal parasite shedding in raccoons, while nematode transmission remains unaffected by fecal pile density.
Contextual materials: Wildlife species are host to a variety of gastrointestinal parasites (GIPs). Artificially concentrating animals may increase the risk of disease spread due to increased GIP load and associated environmental load. Supplemental feeding of deer is common among hunters and known to concentrate animals, but there is limited knowledge of how it a ects GIP environmental load. GIP load was compared between ecologically-equivalent pairs of sites in Mississippi with and without year-round supplemental feeding (average distance between pairs = 147 m). During May-August in 2019 and 2020, feces from white-tailed deer and raccoons were collected and examined for the presence of nematodes, coccidia, Giardia spp., Cryptosporidium spp., and Baylisascaris procyonis. On average, fed sites had 8 more deer (241% increase) and 2 more raccoon fecal piles (540% increase) than unfed sites. Average parasite loads for individual fecal samples did not di er between fed and unfed sites, but the greater number of deer and raccoon fecal piles at fed sites (p < 0.0001) produced 231% and 308% greater environmental loads of nematodes and coccidia, respectively. Spin feeders, the only feeder type that distributed feed on the ground, had 326% more coccidia in feces on average compared to other feeder types (p < 0.03). These results show that supplemental feeding of white-tailed deer, especially with spin feeders, increases environmental loads of GIP and the potential for transmission of parasitic diseases.

question: In a dairy cow with severe abomasal ulcerative disease evaluated microscopically after necropsy, which histopathological pattern would best indicate a type 5 ulcer instead of a superficial type 1 lesion or a perforated type 3 or 4 ulcer?
A: Superficial necrosis limited mainly to mucus-secreting mucous cells with minimal inflammatory response.
B: Chronic ulceration with three zones consisting of an inflammatory necrotic bed, granulation tissue, and dense submucosal fibrosis.
C: Widespread necrosis extending from the mucosa through to the serosa with loss of glandular and vascular structures.
D: Extensive necrosis accompanied by fibrosis, consistent with a perforated ulcer but without generalized loss of glandular and vascular architecture.
Contextual materials: While imaging and surgical exploration provide valuable structural insights, histopathological analysis remains essential for understanding the underlying tissue-level pathology of abomasal ulcers. As previously mentioned, one of the main limitations in this case is the lack of histopathological sampling. Histopathology is a highly valuable diagnostic method for the definitive evaluation of gastrointestinal lesions observed during the autopsy. In a study by De Andrade Neto et al. involving the histopathological examination of 201 abomasal ulcer fragments, the most common type 1 ulcer lesions included superficial necrosis of mucous cells with minor inflammation—sometimes presenting solely as the loss of mucus-secreting cells. Other findings included acute necrosis extending to the muscularis due to mucosal plate damage and chronic necrosis reaching the submucosa and muscular layers, forming three distinct zones: necrotic and inflammatory ulcer bed, granulation tissue, and dense fibrotic tissue with vascular changes in the submucosa. Some lesions also showed glandular atrophy with mild submucosal inflammation. In another study by the same author, which examined type 3, 4, and 5 ulcers, type 3 and 4 perforated ulcers were characterized by extensive necrosis with fibrosis, while type 5 ulcers exhibited widespread necrosis extending from the mucosa to the serosa, accompanied by the loss of glandular and vascular structures. Similarly, a study by Yasaswini et al. identified mucosal infiltration by inflammatory cells, multifocal necrosis, degeneration, erosion, and loss of muscle architecture. However, the specific ulcer types were not stated in that study. Given the limited data available on the histopathological features of abomasal ulcers, future cases of this kind should include a histological examination as a standard diagnostic procedure to better understand the etiology and progression of slug ulcers.

question: When assessing two genetically related equid hemoparasites that produce similar acute signs, including hemolytic anemia, fever, anorexia, and prostration, one is mildly virulent in immunocompetent horses and resistant to imidocarb dipropionate, while the other can cause severe disease, may be fatal, and is usually imidocarb susceptible. If an experimental study shows that Haemaphysalis longicornis does not transmit the mildly virulent, imidocarb-resistant parasite transstadially, what conclusion is best supported scientifically?
A: Haemaphysalis longicornis should also be considered incapable of transmitting the more virulent imidocarb-susceptible parasite because the two parasites are genetically closely related.
B: Failure to transmit the mildly virulent parasite establishes that Rhipicephalus microplus is the only biologically competent vector for both equid parasites.
C: The finding rules out future epidemiologic risk from Haemaphysalis longicornis because tick adaptation to new environments cannot alter pathogen transmission capacity.
D: The result demonstrates lack of vector competence for that parasite under the study conditions but does not determine whether Haemaphysalis longicornis can transmit the related, more virulent parasite.
Contextual materials: Theileria haneyi is genetically closely related to T. equi, with both hemoparasites infecting equids and causing similar clinical signs during acute infection, including hemolytic anemia, fever, anorexia, and prostration. However, there are marked diferences between these two parasites. Whereas experimental studies have shown that T. haneyi is only mildly virulent to immunocompetent horses, experimental and field data show that T. equi causes severe anemia and fever and can be lethal in some cases. In addition, T. haneyi is resistant to imidocarb dipropionate, the drug of choice for treating equine piroplasmosis, whereas T. equi is susceptible to this drug, with only sporadic cases of resistance being reported. Experimental studies have demonstrated that Rhipicephalus microplus ticks are competent vectors for transmitting T. equi. However, given that R. microplus are monoxenic ticks and that horses are not natural hosts to this species, the epidemiological implications of this finding remain to be determined. Currently, no information is available on whether R. microplus is competent in transmitting T. haneyi. Therefore, considering these biological diferences between T. haneyi and T. equi, which specific characteristics would allow or prevent these parasites from being transmitted by a particular tick species remains unknown. Thus, although in the present study, we showed that H. longicornis is not a competent vector for the transstadial transmission of T. haneyi, whether this tick species is a competent vector for T. equi remains to be determined. Furthermore, the present findings do not rule out the possibility that as H. longicornis becomes more widespread and adapted to new environments, such as the eastern, northern, and southern USA, it may acquire the capacity to transmit T. haneyi to equids, as well as new pathogens to humans, livestock, and wildlife.

question: When using a long-acting anthelmintic in pre-lambing ewes to limit periparturient nematode egg shedding while reducing selection for resistance, which approach is most appropriate for maintaining parasites in refugia, especially in sheep with a short post-parturient relaxation of immunity?
A: Administer the long-acting product sufficiently before lambing so its residual activity has ended by the time ewe immunity recovers, and avoid treating a small proportion of ewes.
B: Administer the long-acting product close to lambing so its declining activity overlaps with rapid recovery of ewe immunity and kills newly ingested larvae.
C: Treat all ewes with repeated long-acting doses throughout lactation to prevent any susceptible larvae from surviving on pasture.
D: Delay treatment until after immunity has fully recovered so only parasites in highly immune hosts are exposed to the product.
Contextual materials: Anthelmintics are likely to select more strongly for resistance when given to immune animals or those which regain their immunity while the product is still active, as well as during the ‘tail’ phase of anthelmintic activity when new larvae are ingested post-treatment. The ‘tail’ phase should not coincide with the recovery of immunity in the ewe. It is therefore important that the long-acting wormer is given to the ewe sufficiently long before lambing so that the effects are no longer present when the ewe’s immunity returns to its previous level in order to maintain an in refugia population. This must be particularly born in mind with breeds of sheep which have a shorter PPRI period such as Romneys. Another means of achieving sufficient refugia population would be to only treat a proportion of the ewes. The SCOPS guidelines suggest treating 90% of ewes prior to lambing when using a long-acting formulation. Guidelines on the responsible use of moxidectin have been created in conjunction with SCOPS in order to help delay the development of anthelmintic resistance.

question: Which conclusion most appropriately combines the injection-site and liver histopathology results from a rabbit safety study in which subcutaneous extended-release meloxicam at placebo, 4, 12, and 20 mg/kg produced comparable local inflammation across groups (one-way ANOVA p = 0.899), while mild portal or sinusoidal extramedullary hematopoiesis in the liver tended to be higher at 12 and 20 mg/kg without a statistically significant group difference (one-way ANOVA p = 0.078)?
A: The formulation caused a clear local injection-site reaction, but there was no evidence of any systemic tissue response.
B: The formulation did not produce a detectable injection-site reaction, while the liver findings suggest a mild possible systemic hematopoietic effect that was not statistically significant or severe.
C: The liver lesions establish dose-dependent hepatocellular necrosis, and the injection-site findings confirm concurrent chemical cellulitis.
D: The lack of significant differences in both tissues proves that all observed inflammatory and hematopoietic findings were unrelated spontaneous artifacts.
Contextual materials: The histopathological evaluation revealed that subcutaneous inflammation, characterized by mixed inflammatory cell infiltrates as well as fibroblast proliferation and edema, was comparable across all groups, including both placebo and Meloxicam-SC-XR-treated animals, as depicted in Figure 3. Mean ± SD values of subcutaneous inflammation scores for placebo and treatment groups 4 mg/kg, 12 mg/ kg, and 20 mg/kg were 1.75 ± 0.9, 1.75 ± 1.5, 2.00 ± 0.8, and $2 . 2 5 \pm 0 . 9 ,$ respectively. There was no significant diference in subcutaneous inflammation between the groups (One-way ANOVA, p = 0.899). This indicated that the meloxicam formulation did not elicit an injection site reaction, supporting its safety for subcutaneous administration. In contrast, a mild increase in liver extramedullary hematopoiesis (EMH), which featured white or blood cell precursors, was present in the portal areas or sinusoids in meloxicam-treated groups, particularly at higher doses (12 mg/kg and 20 mg/kg), compared to the placebo group. Mean ± SD values of EMH scores for placebo and treatment groups 4 mg/kg, 12 mg/kg, and 20 mg/kg were $0 . 7 5 \pm 0 . 5 , 1 . 5 \pm 0 . 6 , 2 . 0 0 \pm 0 . 8 ,$ and $2 . 0 0 \pm 0 . 8$ , respectively. There was no significant diference in EMH between the groups (One-way $\mathrm { A N O V A } , p = 0 . 0 7 8 )$ . While this may indicate a potential systemic hematopoietic efect, the changes remained mild and were not indicative of severe pathology.

question: Wild carnivores with histologic meningoencephalitis have lesion patterns consistent with a viral cause, yet severe clinical signs of CNS disease are absent. Broad immunohistochemical and molecular testing for established and novel carnivore viruses yields negative results. In six affected brain samples examined by viral metagenomics, two show only very low numbers of reads closest to Anelloviridae, while four show no significant viral reads. What conclusion is best supported?
A: The findings strongly establish Anelloviridae as the primary cause of the encephalitis because any viral read in inflamed CNS tissue is etiologically definitive.
B: The negative immunohistochemical results rule out all viral etiologies, including low-copy or divergent viruses detectable only by sequencing approaches.
C: The absence of high viral read counts makes a high-titer viral infection in the sampled tissue unlikely, while a low-load infection or incidental/epiphenomenal Anelloviridae detection remains possible.
D: The lack of overt neurologic signs excludes viral encephalitis because clinically silent CNS inflammation cannot have infectious morphology.
Contextual materials: Furthermore, there has been a considerable number of animals with encephalitis of undetectable cause. A detailed neurological investigation was not performed and neurological dysfunctions or behavioural impairment cannot be ruled out. However, severe neurological impairment or clinical signs indicating CNS disease were not detected in trapped animals or reported by hunters. The morphology of these CNS lesions pointed clearly to a viral etiology. Nevertheless, no causative agents were detected in any of the cases despite undertaking extensive immunohistochemical investigations and advanced molecular analysis to detect commonly known as well as new viral pathogens in carnivores. Of interest, analysis of the brain tissues of six animals with meningo-encephalitis by viral metagenomics revealed very low numbers, with the closest similarity to members of the Anelloviridae in two samples, while no significant viral reads were detected in the other four brain tissues samples. These findings indicate that it is unlikely that a high virus load was present in the tested tissue. However, it cannot be ruled out that an infection with a low viral load was present in the tested tissues, which could be detected with other, novel NGS methods. This might be a promising approach for further investigations. The evidence of readings with similarities to Anelloviridae is of interest, as they have a high prevalence in the human population and are associated with hepatitis or pathological conditions of the respiratory tract or immune system. Namely, there exist some reports highlighting the disease-inducing potential of Anelloviridae. Furthermore, they have also been detected in different animal species, thus leading to the hypothesis that they can be transmitted to humans and vice versa. However, regarding their ubiquitous distribution and their unresolved pathogenicity, it is more likely that their detection only represents a secondary, epiphenomal response. question: In diarrheic beef calves with intestinal protozoa detected during microbiome assessment, which interpretation most clearly separates protozoa associated with dysbiosis from those that may correspond to potentially beneficial microbial community characteristics?
A: Blastocystis and Entamoeba are most consistent with decreased microbial richness and loss of methanogenic archaea, whereas Eimeria, Cryptosporidium, and Giardia intestinalis are markers of increased probiotic bacterial abundance.
B: Cryptosporidium and Giardia intestinalis are expected to increase bacterial evenness and archaeal abundance, whereas Blastocystis and Entamoeba primarily damage the intestinal barrier and deplete commensal bacteria.
C: All intestinal protozoa in diarrheic calves should be interpreted uniformly as causes of reduced bacterial diversity and reduced methanogenic archaea, because protozoal presence has no parasite-specific microbiome association.
D: Eimeria, Cryptosporidium, and Giardia intestinalis are most consistent with reduced barrier integrity or microbial diversity, whereas Blastocystis and Entamoeba may correlate with greater microbial richness and methanogenic archaea.
Contextual materials: Calf diarrhea was often characterized by an imbalance in intestinal fora, and this study also revealed intestinal microbial imbalance in calves with diarrhea. Moreover, Eimeria, Cryptosporidium, and Giardia intestinalis were related to an imbalance in gut microbes. Previous studies have also shown negative effects of these parasites on gut microbes. For example, Eimeria damaged the chicken intestinal barrier and reduced the abundance of probiotic bacteria. Cryptosporidium infection decreased bacterial diversity, and Giardia infection was associated with signifcant dysbiosis within the murine foregut and hindgut. By contrast, Blastocystis and Entamoeba in this study were associated with the diversity of other intestinal microorganisms. Te same phenomenon has been observed in humans, where it was found that Blastocystis was associated with both higher richness and higher evenness of the gut bacterial microbiota, whereas Entamoeba was associated only with higher richness, all of which have a role in maintaining intestinal health. It is worth noting that Blastocystis and Entamoeba were signifcantly positively correlated with various methanogenic archaea. Te possible use of methanogens as probiotics has received particular attention in humans; therefore, the positive relationship between Blastocystis, Entamoeba, and methanogenic archaea may be benefcial for gut health. Te relationship between archaea and parasites in animals has received little attention, and more research is needed to uncover this phenomenon.

question: During the early grazing phase of a lamb study involving Haemonchus contortus, fecal egg counts were comparable between two groups, and grass next to fecal deposits showed similarly high L3 contamination. Yet random herbage samples contained about 21 times more L3 on the natural meadow than on the chicory-recultivated plot. What is the best explanation for this difference?
A: Chicory likely impaired survival or migration of free-living H. contortus larvae on pasture, potentially through plant structure and bioactive phenolic compounds affecting larval development.
B: Chicory most likely reduced establishment of adult H. contortus in the lambs, causing lower egg shedding that was not reflected in fecal egg counts.
C: The natural meadow plot most likely had lower larval migration from feces onto herbage, concentrating L3 near fecal deposits rather than on random grass samples.
D: The difference is best explained by a diagnostic artifact because L3 contamination on random pasture samples should directly mirror fecal egg counts when host exposure is similar.
Contextual materials: Our study of changes in the level of pasture contamination with H. contortus L3 provided interesting results. The level of contamination with L3 on both pasture plots increased in the first stage of the experiment (until D41), which was associated with the peculiarities of the development of H. contortus in the environment. L3 contamination of the “random” pasture grass, however, was 20.9-fold higher on the CON than the CHIC plot, despite the similarity of the EPG values in the CON and CHIC lambs during this period and the similar high contamination of grass “near the feces” around the sheepfolds (Table 2). This diference in the contamination of the pasture plots may have been due to the lower survival of L3 on the plot recultivated with chicory compared to the natural meadow grass. Haemonchus contortus L3 survives and migrates diferently in pastures with diferent types of vegetation, probably due to the peculiarities of the composition of the vegetation species and the structure of the meadow plant species. The physiological and morphological peculiarities of chicory may hinder larval survival on pasture. We also believe that several bioactive compounds and phenolic metabolites in lamb feces also influence the successful development of eggs and freeliving larvae in the feces. The number of phenolic metabolites in our study was higher in the feces of the CHIC than in the CON lambs (Figures 2, 3). Chicory and its extracts negatively afect the development of eggs and larvae of various ruminants, so we believe that the decrease in the level of pasture contamination with L3 in our study was associated with the influence of bioactive plants, mainly chicory.

question: During a field study of chickens given fluralaner in drinking water at 0.5 mg/kg body weight as two doses separated by 7 days, prior poultry red mite data suggested complete mite mortality for roughly 5 days after each dose and full protection through about day 12 after the first treatment. In open-sided housing accessible to wild birds, treated birds were free of northern fowl mites by day 14, yet a few mites were found on some treated birds on days 19 and 28. What is the best interpretation of these later observations?
A: They indicate that fluralaner failed to reach therapeutic concentrations after the second dose, because mites persisted continuously through day 14.
B: They most likely represent reinfestation after the post-treatment protective period had ended, facilitated by continued environmental or wild-bird exposure.
C: They demonstrate development of complete fluralaner resistance during the initial 5 days after treatment, causing immediate survival of the original mite population.
D: They show that northern fowl mites are unaffected by fluralaner when it is administered in drinking water, regardless of dose timing.
Contextual materials: Fluralaner administered to chickens in drinking water at the 0.5 mg/kg BW dose used in this study provided 100% mortality of poultry red mite for up to 5 days with a second administered dose 7 days after the frst, extending the 100% mortality period another 5 days (to 12 days after the frst treatment). If the protective period for NFM is similar to that reported for poultry red mite, reinfestation of treated birds by NFM might be expected after the 5-day protective period following the last administration of furalaner. Indeed, in the feld efcacy study where study birds were housed in open-sided poultry houses allowing access by wild birds and thus continuous opportunity for NFM reinfestation, a small number of NFM were observed on a few treated birds at days 19 and 28 following the earlier elimination of NFM by day 14.

question: After a dog is given the candidate antimicrobial AB4 subcutaneously at 20 mg/kg once daily for seven days, pharmacokinetic results show an accumulation ratio under 2, a fluctuation index of 1 to 3, slight but nonsignificant increases in half-life and apparent volume of distribution versus single dosing, and a relatively high mean peak-to-trough ratio at steady state. What is the most appropriate clinical interpretation for dosing based on these findings?
A: AB4 shows marked time-dependent accumulation, so all dogs should receive a longer dosing interval after the first dose to prevent progressive toxicity.
B: AB4 has statistically significant prolongation of half-life after repeated dosing, so therapeutic precision is best achieved by reducing dosing frequency in recovering dogs.
C: AB4 maintains a generally stable multiple-dose pharmacokinetic profile, but acute severe disease may justify a higher initial dose or more frequent dosing to reach therapeutic concentrations promptly.
D: AB4 exhibits negligible peak-to-trough variation at steady state, so the same fixed dose and interval should be used for acute, severe, mild, and recovery-phase cases.
Contextual materials: Under repeated subcutaneous administration at 20 mg/kg for seven consecutive days, AB4 demonstrated an accumulation ratio <2 and a degree of fluctuation between 1 and 3, indicating no significant accumulation and moderate plasma concentration variability. Although repeated administration led to a slight increase in $t _ { 1 / 2 }$ and volume of distribution compared to single dosing, the diferences were not statistically significant, suggesting that AB4 maintains a stable pharmacokinetic profile upon multiple dosing. However, the mean peak-to-trough concentration ratio at steady state was relatively high. Based on these pharmacokinetic findings, it is recommended that clinical dosing strategies be adjusted accordingly: For acute or severe cases, an increased initial dose or more frequent dosing may be warranted to rapidly achieve therapeutic plasma levels. Conversely, for milder cases or during recovery, a reduced dose with increased dosing frequency may help lower drug burden and improve treatment precision.

question: Given an in vitro assessment of tafenoquine (TFQ) for equine piroplasmosis in which equine PBMC viability remains unchanged through 5 µM but decreases significantly at 10 µM and above, T. equi is inhibited at concentrations near or just above the point where PBMC cytotoxicity begins, complete B. caballi inhibition requires concentrations beyond that cytotoxic threshold, and the selectivity indices are 1.69 for T. equi and 0.69 for B. caballi, which conclusion is most appropriate?
A: TFQ is equally suitable for treating both T. equi and B. caballi because PBMC cytotoxicity begins only after both parasites are completely inhibited.
B: TFQ should be prioritized for B. caballi because a selectivity index below 1 indicates parasite-specific toxicity with minimal host-cell risk.
C: TFQ lacks any meaningful antiparasitic potential against T. equi because a selectivity index of 1.69 proves that host-cell toxicity occurs before parasite inhibition.
D: TFQ has a more favorable, though still suboptimal, safety margin against T. equi than against B. caballi, making it a better candidate for refinement or combination strategies targeting T. equi.
Contextual materials: TFQ demonstrated no signifcant cytotoxicity in equine PBMCs at concentrations up to 5 µM. Cell viability began to decline only at concentrations ≥ 10 µM (P < 0.05), which falls within or slightly above the efective antiparasitic range for T. equi, but remained below the concentration required for complete inhibition of B. caballi. Te SSI of TFQ was nearly twice as high for T. equi as for host cells. In contrast, the SSI for B. caballi was only 0.69, indicating that the therapeutic concentrations required to inhibit this species either approach or exceed the cytotoxic threshold in PBMCs. Tese fndings highlight TFQ’s more favorable safety margin and selectivity against T. equi, while also underscoring its narrower therapeutic window for B. caballi. It is important to note that although the SSI of 1.69 against T. equi falls below the threshold typically desired for lead optimization, it still provides a meaningful indication of diferential activity and supports TFQ’s potential as a starting point for further structural refnement or combination strategies. Collectively, this underscores that the SSI should be interpreted in conjunction with other pharmacological parameters and the established mechanisms of action of TFQ. Tis profle is consistent with a previous study in human THP-1 cells, where TFQ demonstrated a relatively high median lethal dose $\mathrm { ( L D _ { 5 0 } ) }$ of $5 3 . 5 7 ~ \mu \mathrm { M } ,$ indicating its preferential toxicity toward parasites over host cells. Although TFQ has been associated with hemolytic toxicity in G6PD-defcient human erythrocytes, only a single case of G6PD defciency has been reported in equines, unrelated to TFQ-induced hemolysis. Tis suggests that although G6PD defciency may have limited clinical relevance in horses, its signifcance remains uncertain and warrants further investigation.

question: In a year-long comparison of diploid and triploid tench that assesses parasite abundance, gonadosomatic index, leukocyte count, and phagocyte respiratory burst, which pattern of findings most strongly indicates that triploidy is broadly protective while affecting different parasite species unevenly rather than lowering every metazoan infection uniformly?
A: Triploid tench have a lower overall parasite load and lower abundance of the host-specific adult trematode Asymphylodora tincae, but a higher abundance of the larval cestode Valipora campylancristrota and similar infection intensity with Gyrodactylus tincae.
B: Triploid tench have higher abundance of all specialist parasites, lower abundance of all generalist parasites, and no measurable differences in immune or hematological variables.
C: Diploid and triploid tench have identical infection parameters for all parasite taxa, but triploids show consistently higher gonadosomatic index and reduced leukocyte counts.
D: Triploid tench have uniformly lower abundance of trematodes, cestodes, monogeneans, and myxosporeans, with no association between reproductive investment and infection risk.
Contextual materials: In conclusion, our study demonstrated that the ploidy status in tench afected metazoan parasite infection, reproductive investment (measured by GSI), haematological parameters, and immune function (specifically, leukocyte count and phagocyte activity expressed by respiratory burst). We revealed that triploids tended to have lower parasite load than diploids throughout the year. Nevertheless, our findings indicate that polyploidy exerts non-uniform efects on infection by diferent parasite species. Triploids exhibited lower abundance of the host-specific adult trematode A. tincae, yet significantly higher abundance of the larval cestode V. campylancristrota. Highly prevalent and moderately abundant monogenean specialist G. tincae was found in triploids and diploids at the similar intensity of infection. The other parasite species exhibited generally low infection parameters. We also identified an association between parasite infection and gonadosomatic condition, indicating that increased reproductive investment may elevate infection risk, particularly in diploid tench. Our results suggest potential efects of the three most abundant parasite taxa (Gyrodactylus tincae, Asymphylodora tincae and Myxosporea spp.) on tench immunity. The observed diferences in parasite infection between triploid and diploid tench and the associations between parasite load and condition- and health-related traits may be explained by several factors: (1) presumed higher heterozygosity in triploids, (2) physiological diferences related to cell size and number of cells in key organs and tissues, (3) variation in feeding performance, and (4) host–parasite coevolutionary interactions between diploid tench and their associated parasites.

question: In a suburban domestic cat lacking known exposure to wild non-human primates, chronic ulcerative skin wounds contain Trichuris/Capillaria-like capillariid eggs on microscopic examination of superficial lesion material. What is the most appropriate diagnostic interpretation and epidemiologic conclusion?
A: Trichuris trichiura is the most likely cause because its eggs are commonly found in feline skin ulcers and non-human primates are not relevant to its maintenance.
B: Anatrichosoma spp. should be included as a differential diagnosis because it can produce cutaneous infections, and eggs shed from ulcerative lesions may contaminate soil as a possible transmission source.
C: Cutaneous capillariid eggs should be interpreted as environmental contaminants only, because capillarids are unable to produce superficial or subcutaneous lesions in animals.
D: Absence of contact with wild non-human primates rules out Anatrichosoma infection because transmission requires direct exposure to primate reservoir hosts.
Contextual materials: Because the lifecycle of Anatrichosoma spp. is unclear, the transmission and reservoir host are poorly known. However, Anatrichosoma spp. commonly afects non-human primates, suggesting that such primates are reservoir hosts for Anatrichosoma spp. Interestingly, this cat was raised in a suburban area and had no contact with any wild non-human primates. Anatrichosoma eggs were presented in ulcerative wounds. The eggs might contaminate the soil, and transmission via contact with contaminated soil should, therefore, be considered. Because Trichuris trichiura eggs have been reported in oral mucosal lesions in a child in Brazil, it has been suggested that Anatrichosoma spp. should be in the diferential diagnosis list when Capillaria-like eggs were found in superficial cutaneous and subcutaneous sites from these animals. None of these capillarids can cause cutaneous lesions, whereas Anatrichosoma spp. can lead to cutaneous infections in pets and wild species.

question: After neonatal bovine polymorphonuclear neutrophils (PMN) are exposed to Cryptosporidium parvum oocysts and sporozoites in a laboratory study, early activation is assessed. Live-cell 3D holotomographic microscopy within 10 minutes reveals more pseudopod formation, chemotaxis, cytoplasmic granule movement, and membrane protrusions, while separate staining shows increased F-actin polymerization. What is the best functional interpretation of these PMN findings?
A: The PMN are primarily entering apoptosis, as indicated by loss of cytoskeletal organization and nuclear fragmentation after parasite contact.
B: The PMN are differentiating into macrophage-like phagocytes, as shown by increased cell diameter and replacement of multilobulated nuclei with round nuclei.
C: The PMN are undergoing cytoskeletal remodeling that supports activation-associated processes such as degranulation and neutrophil extracellular trap formation.
D: The PMN are becoming functionally quiescent, because F-actin polymerization prevents chemotaxis and inhibits granule mobilization.
Contextual materials: At first, we evaluated the activation of C. parvum-confronted neonatal bovine PMN through F-actin polymerization as an indication of cytoskeleton changes that are involved in processes such as degranulation and NET formation. Our results show that cytoskeleton remodeling is an important step in neonatal PMN activation, as it also occurs in adult-derived PMN. The cytoskeleton rearrangement accompanied by movement of the granules, crawling, and pseudopod formation was evident when the C. parvum-confronted neonatal bovine PMN were analyzed by live cell 3D holotomographic microscopy. This technique permits detailed cell morphometric analysis and observation of cellular processes during the NETosis process, as reported elsewhere. Current data show that neonatal bovine PMN reacted to the addition of C. parvum oocysts and sporozoites within the first 10 min by increased pseudopod formation, chemotaxis, and movement of cytoplasmic granules and membrane protrusions. These results correlate with previous observations of adult PMN reacting against other apicomplexan parasites such as B. besnoiti bradyzoites. In addition, the morphometric analysis indicates that neonatal bovine PMN have an average diameter of 8.93 ± 1.46 µm and are smaller in size when compared with the reported average size of adult bovine PMN of 10–12 µm. Finally, the multilobulated nature of the PMN nuclei was also observed in both unstimulated and C. parvum-confronted neonatal PMN when the nuclear staining DRAQ5 was used. This is in line with several reports of neonatal PMN of humans and mice indicating no obvious diferences in nuclear morphology between species or with adult bovine PMN.

question: Several pregnant ewes abort 10 days after exposure to Toxoplasma gondii oocysts. Necropsy reveals marked thrombosis and infarction in the placentomes, while no parasites are found in placental or fetal tissues and T. gondii-specific IgG is absent in some dams at abortion. What is the best interpretation of this pattern?
A: A late toxoplasmosis-associated abortion syndrome caused by fetal immune control of parasite replication leading to multifocal placental necrosis.
B: A noninfectious nutritional abortion syndrome, because absence of detectable parasites and maternal IgG excludes toxoplasmosis during acute gestation.
C: A chronic congenital toxoplasmosis syndrome in which persistent fetal infection produces weak lambs after late-gestation exposure.
D: An early toxoplasmosis-associated abortion syndrome likely driven by acute infection and an exaggerated proinflammatory response causing placental thrombosis.
Contextual materials: Te outcome of T. gondii infection in pregnant sheep is highly dependent on the gestational stage at which infection occurs: infection during the frst two-thirds of pregnancy usually results in resorption or abortion, whereas infection during late pregnancy usually results in stillbirth or birth of weak lambs due to partial control of parasite replication by the developing foetal immune system. In any case, two clinical presentations of toxoplasmosis-related abortions have been described in sheep, distinguished by the timing post-infection (dpi) when abortions occur: early abortion (7–14 dpi) and late abortion (28 dpi onwards). Early abortions have been described in experimental infections in sheep, but also in goats, and might be underdiagnosed in the feld, as, unlike late abortions, early abortions often lack detectable parasites in the placenta or foetal tissues, as well as T. gondii-specifc IgG antibodies in the dam at the time of abortion. Moreover, histological lesions in the placenta difer between both clinical presentations: while early abortions are characterised by thrombotic lesions and infarcts in placentomes, late abortions are characterized by multifocal necrosis. Several investigations in the last decade have shown that early abortions may occur after sheep are infected at diferent stages of gestation with diferent T. gondii genotypes and even after infection with as few as 10 sporulated oocysts. Te pathogenic mechanism underlying early abortion remains unclear, although it is hypothesised that placental thrombosis leading to early abortion results from an exacerbated proinfammatory immune response triggered in tissues involved in the early dynamics of infection, such as the small intestine and mesenteric lymph nodes, following parasite replication during acute infection.

question: In a molecular survey of ectoparasites from parti-coloured bats, investigators tested bat-associated fleas, argasid ticks, and Steatonyssus mites for filarial nematode DNA. Only Steatonyssus spinosus mites were positive for microfilarial DNA, while fleas from the same host individuals tested negative, and earlier studies have suggested macronyssid mesostigmatid mites as possible vectors of filarial larvae in other mammals. What conclusion is best supported by these findings?
A: Steatonyssus spinosus should be regarded as a plausible candidate vector, but detection of parasite DNA alone does not demonstrate vector competence or successful transmission.
B: Fleas can be excluded as filarial vectors in bats generally because negative PCR results from fleas on the same hosts prove biological incapacity to transmit filariae.
C: Steatonyssus spinosus is confirmed as the definitive host of the filarial nematode because parasite DNA was detected in the mite rather than in other ectoparasites.
D: Argasid ticks are the most likely vectors because their hematophagous feeding biology makes molecular detection unnecessary for assigning transmission roles.
Contextual materials: Very little is known about the filarial nematode life-cycle transmission phase in bats, and their invertebrate vectors are poorly understood. Bats host a wide variety of ectoparasites, including those that we tested using molecular methods, i.e., fleas (Siphonaptera: Ischnopsyllidae), ticks (Ixodida: Argasidae: Carios), and mites of the genus Steatonyssus (Mesostigmata: Macronyssidae). In this study, we showed that only S. spinosus mites were positive for presence of microfilarial DNA. As fleas collected from the same individual tested negative, this suggests that S. spinosus may be a potential vector. This may be supported by previous suggestion that mites of the order Mesostigmata may be potential vectors of larval filariae stages, while macronyssid mites are thought to be a vector of Litomosoides in rodents, marsupials and bats. This hypothesis of transmission by macronyssid mites is also supported by experimental introduction of Ornithonyssus bacoti onto the microfilaraemic Parnell’s mustached bat (Pteronotus parnellii) and the Jamaican fruit bat (Artibeus jamaicensis). The most common ectoparasite of V. murinus, S. spinosus, is recorded throughout most of the species’ range and is characterized by a high degree of adherence to the host and relatively strong host specificity. They parasitise their hosts in the summer roosts, with some species becoming permanent parasites. Moreover, a related Steatonyssus species, S. periblepharus, has recently been suggested as a novel potential vector of the bat parasite Trypanosoma dionisii. Interestingly, such wing membrane mites may also serve as vectors of some other infectious agents, such as the white-nose syndrome fungus. Nevertheless, the sole presence of DNA in S. spinosus does not prove that this ectoparasite serves as a vector of the detected parasites, and experimental studies are needed to assess its role in the epidemiology of bat infecting filarial nematodes.

question: In a goat pharmacokinetic milk-residue study, a milk withdrawal interval (WDI) is estimated from data for 5 goats. A Monte Carlo method then generates 5 additional virtual goats using only the goats that had measurable milk drug concentrations at the fourth terminal-phase sampling point, 47 hours after the final dose, while excluding goats below the 4 ng/mL detection limit at that time. Relative to simulating extra replicate observations from the complete dataset, which methodological effect is most likely from generating virtual animals this way?
A: It biases the simulated population toward faster milk residue depletion, potentially shortening the WDI below the true safe interval.
B: It biases the simulated population toward slower milk residue depletion, potentially producing a more conservative WDI.
C: It eliminates terminal-phase variability because all concentrations below the detection limit are replaced by a fixed numerical value.
D: It improves external validity by ensuring that simulated animals represent both rapid and slow eliminators equally.
Contextual materials: When comparing the calculated milk WDI between Scenario 1 and Scenario 2 (simulating 5 additional animals from a 5-animal dataset), there was a 12 h diference (i.e., 70.1 vs. 82.8 h) in estimated WDI, resulting in a slightly diferent WDI recommendation (72 h for Scenario 1 and 84 h for Scenario 2). The small diference between Scenario 1 and Scenario 2 can be attributed to the fourth terminal phase time point in the simulated five virtual goats. The base animals (Goats 1, 2, 3, 4, and 8) used to simulate the 5 additional animals were those that had measurable milk concentrations at the fourth terminal phase time point (mean concentration of 19.76 ng/mL and a coeficient of variation (CV) of 43%), which excludes the animals from the additional dataset that had milk concentrations below the LOD (4 ng/mL). By using only animals with measurable concentrations at the fourth terminal phase time point (47 h after the final administered dose), the WDI produced by Scenario 2 was biased towards the slower eliminating animals and therefore produced a more conservative WDI for drugs with more rapid milk residue depletion. In the present study, the diference was minimal, i.e., \~12 h. However, the exact diference will depend on the milk depletion profile of the specific drug in a particular species. Moreover, drugs that have prolonged or irregular estimated milk depletion kinetics may have more pronounced diferences in WDI variability between actual data and simulated data approaches. These results suggest that, depending on the animal population, sampling scheme, and data selection, using the Monte Carlo simulation technique to generate additional virtual animal data introduces relatively more variability to the final predicted milk WDI when compared to simulating additional replicate data.

question: After beginning oral phenobarbital therapy for seizure control, a dog initially shows rising plasma drug concentrations over the first few days, followed by a gradual decrease over the next several weeks even though the dose is unchanged and owner compliance is good. Which pharmacokinetic mechanism best explains these findings?
A: A linear one-compartment model, in which phenobarbital concentrations increase monotonically until reaching a dose-proportional steady state after 5–7 half-lives.
B: A two-compartment distribution model, in which delayed redistribution from peripheral tissues progressively lowers total body clearance over time.
C: A one-compartment model with time-dependent autoinduction, in which phenobarbital progressively increases apparent clearance by reducing degradation of metabolizing enzymes.
D: A saturable elimination model, in which phenobarbital concentrations fall because hepatic metabolic capacity becomes progressively overwhelmed at therapeutic doses.
Contextual materials: The selected structural model was a one-compartment model with an elimination process subject to autoinduction, in which CL/F increases progressively over time. This type of model, previously proposed by Smythe et al. and Hassan et al., simulates the upregulation of metabolizing enzymes as a result of their degradation being inhibited by the drug. The $\mathrm { I C } _ { 5 0 }$ parameter represents the PB concentration that reduces enzyme degradation rate by 50% and plays a central role in capturing the system’s dynamics and adequately simulating progressive enzyme induction. This mechanism helps explain the plasma concentration profiles observed after treatment initiation or dose adjustments with PB. Initially, concentrations rises due to drug accumulation, but then progressively decline as PB induces the expression of metabolizing enzymes. This increase in CL stabilizes over time, such that at steady state, plasma concentrations remain at levels lower than those reached during the first days of treatment. This behavior contrasts with linear pharmacokinetics, where concentrations gradually rise until stabilizing at a level proportional to the administered dose, typically within 5–7 elimination half-lives. The autoinductive structural model captured this temporal pattern accurately, whereas linear models, though statistically acceptable, failed to represent the observed dynamic or provide a mechanistic explanation. Moreover, the autoinductive model yielded better fit metrics, supporting its selection as a more realistic predictive tool. Importantly, the use of a one-compartment model is consistent with both biological plausibility and previous evidence. A systematic review by Methaneethorn and Leelakanok, which evaluated 18 pharmacokinetic studies of phenobarbital in humans, found that all employed one-compartment models, even in the presence of rich sampling designs. This reinforces the empirical and translational robustness of our structural model selection.

question: In dairy cows with claw horn disruption lesions, a randomized lameness study evaluated therapeutic trimming alone against therapeutic trimming plus a hoof block on the healthy claw and a 3-day NSAID regimen, measuring lameness, nociceptive response, and lesion severity after 28 days. Since these lesions involve compression of the sole corium with subsequent vascular dysfunction, ischemia, and hemorrhage, which proposed mechanism best accounts for the higher cure rate with the standard treatment protocol?
A: The hoof block increases axial loading of the affected claw, stimulating keratin production, while NSAIDs primarily prevent bacterial invasion of the corium.
B: Therapeutic trimming and NSAIDs induce controlled hemorrhage in the sole corium, which restores perfusion and accelerates granulation tissue formation.
C: The hoof block immobilizes the distal interphalangeal joint, eliminating nociception, while NSAIDs directly reverse ischemic necrosis by increasing hoof capsule vascular density.
D: The hoof block shifts weight-bearing away from the affected claw, reducing corium compression, while NSAIDs reduce local and systemic inflammation to support healing.
Contextual materials: The primary outcome measures in this study were lameness score, nociceptive response (pain sensitivity), and lesion severity score on day 28 after treatment. Apart from these events, the other mechanisms underlying the causal efect of the standard treatment protocol (therapeutic trim, hoof block, and threeday course of NSAID) could not be elucidated in this study. There are several mechanisms through which the positive efects could occur. The underlying events in the pathogenesis of CHDL are the compression of the sole corium and subsequent vascular dysfunction leading to ischemia and hemorrhage. The blocking of the healthy claw reduces the loadbearing and compression of the corium in the afected claw, thereby promoting injury healing. Likewise, the administration of NSAIDs might elicit a direct efect on the corium by reducing systemic and local inflammation in the hoof capsule and promoting healing following reduced loading due to block application. These events might explain the higher cure rates in LTNB compared to LT which received only therapeutic trim.

question: In a pig pharmacology study developing a tilmicosin dosage regimen for a bacterial respiratory pathogen, how should the PK/PD index be selected when the drug has slow terminal elimination in pigs and in vitro data show greater antibacterial effect with increased exposure, despite macrolides often being described with time-dependent concepts?
A: Use AUC24h/MIC, because prolonged elimination makes total 24-hour exposure relative to organism susceptibility a better predictor than relying only on the percentage of time concentrations exceed the MIC.
B: Use peak concentration/MIC, because any drug with concentration-dependent killing should be dosed solely to maximize Cmax regardless of half-life.
C: Use %T > MIC, because macrolide classification alone is sufficient to select a time-dependent PK/PD target even when elimination is slow.
D: Use trough concentration/MIC, because maintaining the lowest concentration above the MIC is the standard efficacy index for all long-half-life antimicrobials.
Contextual materials: It is sometimes confusing to select the best PK/PD parameters to evaluate the eficacy of drugs based on the antibacterial characteristics (time-dependent or concentration-dependent), because the characteristics of the drug itself have a lot to do with it. The classification of drugs is not the only reference for selecting parameters to describe antibacterial efect. For drugs with long elimination halflife, PK/PD parameter $\mathrm { A U C _ { 2 4 h } / M I C }$ is usually appropriate to describe the efect. The $\mathrm { t _ { 1 / 2 \beta } }$ of tilmicosin likely enables T > MIC to adequately suppress regrowth of the predominant bacterial population. This suggests that the $\mathrm { A U C _ { 2 4 h } / M I C }$ is the optimal PK/PD index to predict antibacterial activity. Azithromycin, time-dependent, because of its long elimination half-life, the best parameter for predicting the eficacy is AUC/MIC. The PK/PD parameters describing the efect of florfenicol is $\mathrm { A U C _ { 2 4 h } / M I C }$ for animals with long elimination half-life and %T > MIC could also be adopted for animals with short elimination half-life. In vitro time-kill assays demonstrated a concentration-dependent antibacterial efect of tilmicosin against Haemophilus parasuis. The efect of tilmicosin against Lawsonia intracellularis was concentration-dependent, thus, AUC/MIC was used to formulate the dosage regimen. In the present study, the correlation between the PK/PD index of $\mathrm { A U C _ { 2 4 h } / M I C }$ and antibacterial efect was the highest (R2 = 0.92), which may be due to the slow elimination of tilmicosin in pigs. This is also an important reason why it is inappropriate to use% T > MIC to guide the administration of tilmicosin.

question: From the standpoint of resistance management, why would a manufacturer recommend retreating dogs with a long-acting systemic ectoparasiticide at 45 days, even when pharmacokinetic and efficacy findings show clinical activity lasting through that time rather than waiting until the drug effect is almost depleted?
A: It allows a short drug-free interval that restores susceptibility in ectoparasite populations by removing selection pressure entirely.
B: It minimizes periods in which declining plasma concentrations fall below the therapeutic threshold, reducing survival and selection of partially resistant fleas and ticks.
C: It prevents resistance primarily by exposing fleas and ticks to alternating high and low systemic drug concentrations that disrupt reproduction.
D: It is intended to synchronize retreatment with the average prepatent period of canine flea allergy dermatitis rather than with parasite susceptibility.
Contextual materials: Although pharmacokinetic and efficacy data indicate sustained clinical activity up to 45 days post-administration, data collection was intentionally limited to this period. The decision to adopt a 45-day retreatment interval aligns with resistance management strategies for ectoparasiticides. Flea and tick resistance is a well-documented phenomenon, driven by high reproductive rates and frequent exposure to subtherapeutic drug concentrations, which may result from operational failures or the gradual decline of systemic drug levels in the host. Therefore, maintaining plasma concentrations above the therapeutic threshold throughout the efficacy interval is essential to prevent the survival and selection of partially resistant individuals. The adoption of a 45-day retreatment interval thus represents a prophylactic measure aimed at minimizing the opportunity for selection of new resistant strains, particularly in environments with high infestation pressure.

question: In abattoir-based surveillance for African swine fever in domestic pigs, some pigs that are ASFV-PCR positive show absent or mild clinical signs before slaughter yet have pronounced hemorrhagic lesions on necropsy, and sequencing identifies genotype IX. Similar hemorrhages in the spleen, lymph nodes, kidneys, and lungs, along with pulmonary edema and tracheal exudate, are also seen in some ASFV-PCR-negative pigs. What is the best interpretation for surveillance?
A: Absence of fever or other obvious clinical signs should be used to exclude ASFV infection in slaughter pigs.
B: Hemorrhagic lesions are pathognomonic for ASFV genotype IX and do not require laboratory confirmation.
C: Gross pathologic lesions may be a more useful abattoir screening trigger than clinical signs, but laboratory testing is needed because differential diagnoses can produce similar lesions.
D: Detection of genotype IX implies a chronic ASFV syndrome, so surveillance should focus primarily on chronic wasting and long-term carrier lesions.
Contextual materials: This study was part of a larger project that evaluated African swine fever presentation and distribution in Uganda. To our knowledge this study is the first to describe the clinical signs and pathologic lesions of ASFV and the prevalence of its diferential diagnoses in slaughtered pigs in Uganda. The findings described in this study are based on comprehensive data collected over a period of 13 months at six pig abattoirs that have a wide catchment area in the country. We found mild to moderate clinical signs in ASFV positive pigs and severe pathologic lesions in ASFV positive pigs slaughtered in the Kampala metropolitan area of Uganda. There were generally no signs of chronic ASFV lesions or signs. We also found pigs with no clinical signs. These findings show that the ASFV genotype and strains circulating in Uganda can cause subacute to acute disease in domestic pigs. As part of this project, we analyzed 31 samples by Whole Genome Sequencing, and they were all identified as genotype IX, indicating that ASFV genotype IX is currently circulating in Uganda. The clinical presentation reported in this present study could be associated with genotype IX. It is important to note that the historic ASFV genotype IX has been maintained as genotype 9 in a proposed new genotype classification. Pigs without clinical signs or with mild clinical signs may represent pigs that were exposed and sent for slaughter, potentially as part of outbreak sell-ofs. Since these pigs were slaughtered and not followed over time, it is not clear if they were pre-clinical or if the disease was sub-clinical. Selling of pigs during outbreaks following outbreaks (panic sales) is a commonly reported management strategy used by farmers to reduce economic losses due to ASF. Pig abattoirs in Uganda could be used as surveillance sites for identifying ASF outbreaks and pathologic lesions seem more reliable for syndromic surveillance than clinical signs. However, it is important to note that some pigs that tested negative for ASFV had hemorrhages in the spleen, lymph nodes, kidneys, lungs as well as lung edema and tracheal exudates. This is indicative of the presence of ASFV diferential diagnoses, hence confirmation will require laboratory diagnosis.

question: For dogs receiving oral potentiated sulfonamide combinations such as trimethoprim/sulfadiazine or trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole, free plasma trimethoprim-to-sulfonamide ratios can be near the traditionally proposed 1:19 value soon after administration but vary later in the dosing interval. What pharmacodynamic interpretation is most appropriate?
A: Loss of the 1:19 ratio later in the dosing interval necessarily indicates loss of antibacterial potentiation, so efficacy should be predicted by maintaining that fixed ratio at all times.
B: Because trimethoprim has a short half-life, sulfonamide exposure alone is sufficient to predict efficacy using a standard AUC/MIC index for the sulfonamide component.
C: The changing plasma ratio shows that trimethoprim contributes only when its concentration exceeds its individual MIC, making sub-MIC trimethoprim concentrations pharmacodynamically irrelevant.
D: Potentiated activity can occur across a range of trimethoprim and sulfonamide concentrations, so separate conventional PK/PD indices for each drug may poorly predict combination efficacy.
Contextual materials: The TMP/SDZ and TMP/SMX free plasma concentration ratios were close to the suggested optimal 1:19 ratio only during the first hours after oral administration. Thereafter, the ratios gradually increased, which is consistent with previous studies on TMP/SDZ in dogs. Given the short half-life of TMP, alternative dosing strategies such as additional doses of TMP could potentially later be explored by PK/PD studies. However, the 1:19 ratio most likely reflects an overemphasis on early in vitro observations. rather than a strict in vivo requirement for potentiated antibacterial activity. Indded, both older and more recent studies indicate that synergistic or potentiating interactions between TMP and sulphonamides occur over a range of relative concentrations, rather than at a single fixed ratio of 1:19, and that exposures that deviate from this ratio are also likely to achieve potentiated antibacterial activity in dogs. Such ratio flexibility is likely to be particularly relevant for maintaining antibacterial activity in in vivo conditions, where this study demonstrated that the relative drug concentration ratios change over the dosing interval but also complexifies the PK/PD analysis. A recent study demonstrated that, at any given time, the extent of TMPS synergy depends on the concentrations of both drugs, and that even TMP concentration s up to 22-fold below the MIC can still contribute to synergistic efects. Therefore, conventional PK/PD indices such as T > MIC or AUC/MIC, when applied separately to each drug, are unlikely to accurately predict the eficacy of the combination. This highlights the importance of our study predicting PK profiles of free TMP, SMX and SDZ concentrations after different routes of administration in a dog population. Such data are required to be later integrated with PD data from synergy studies and dynamic in vitro infection models into PK/PD models that will better predict eficacy for diferent potentiated sulphonamides, diferent doses and diferent routes of administration, against canine pathogens such as Staphylococcus pseudintermedius.

question: When solid feed partially substitutes for milk replacer in veal calf diets, rumen development may improve and abnormal oral behaviors may decrease, yet abomasal lesions at slaughter become more common as daily solid-feed intake increases. What explanation most accurately identifies the main mechanism by which present solid-feeding practices lead to these lesions?
A: High starch intake increases fermentable substrate reaching the abomasum, promoting acidification and mucosal damage more strongly than neutral detergent fiber intake does.
B: High neutral detergent fiber intake physically abrades the abomasal mucosa, making fiber particle roughness the dominant determinant of lesion prevalence.
C: Reduced milk replacer intake causes protein deficiency that impairs abomasal epithelial repair, independently of dietary carbohydrate composition.
D: Improved rumen development accelerates gastric emptying enough to cause alkaline reflux injury as the principal cause of abomasal lesions.
Contextual materials: powder, main raw materials used in milk replacer formulations for calves. These price dynamics encouraged the partial substitution of milk replacer with SF. In addition, the shift was supported by scientific evidences, reporting improved performance in veal calves when receiving high levels of SF particularly at the end of the fattening period. The synthesis of the available literature confirmed that providing SF promoted rumen development and reduced abnormal oral behaviors in veal calves. However, the increase amount of their daily intake shifted the welfare challenges for veal calves from behavioural deprivation towards gastrointestinal dysfunction. The meta-regression analysis carried out in this study has shown that this shift has promoted a marked increase in the prevalence of abomasal lesions recorded at slaughter. Moreover, the strong association identified between starch intake and abomasal damage suggests that under current solid feeding practices, the starch load delivered to the abomasum, rather than the physical abrasiveness of dietary fiber, appears the primary driver of abomasal lesions in veal calves. This significant association between increasing starch intake and lesion prevalence, coupled with the absence of a comparable relationship for NDF, indicates that starch-induced acidification is likely a central pathogenic mechanism.

question: In pigs, a sigmoid Emax pharmacodynamic analysis of tulathromycin against Actinobacillus pleuropneumoniae identifies the fraction of the dosing interval with concentrations above the MIC as the main predictor of antibacterial effect. Which approach to dosing and interpretation best matches this time-dependent PK/PD pattern?
A: Design the regimen primarily to maximize peak concentration/MIC, because bactericidal activity is expected once a brief high concentration is achieved regardless of time above MIC.
B: Design the regimen to keep concentrations above the MIC for most of the dosing interval, with about 50.8% T > MIC associated with a 1-log10 CFU/mL reduction and about 96.38% T > MIC associated with bactericidal activity.
C: Design the regimen around total daily AUC/MIC only, because tulathromycin efficacy against A. pleuropneumoniae is independent of whether concentrations remain above the MIC.
D: Assume that ex vivo PK/PD targets directly underestimate in vivo requirements, because host immunity is absent and bacterial load has no effect on the magnitude of PK/PD targets.
Contextual materials: Tulathromycin possessed a characteristic of time dependence against A. pleuropneumoniae and PK/PD-based modeling with the sigmoid $\mathrm { E } _ { \mathrm { m a x } }$ model indicating that animal dose regimens should supply %T > MIC of tulathromycin at least 50.8% to achieve a $1 \mathrm { ~ - ~ } \mathrm { l o g } _ { 1 0 } \mathrm { C F U / m l }$ reduction and 96.38% to achieve a bactericidal efect. We also found that the antibacterial efect was favorably correlated to the time that the drug concentration exceeded MIC and this difered from previous studies. The reasons for these diferences are severalfold; ex vivo and in vivo models possess diferences, the ex vivo model holds the antibiotic concentration constant, and the response was independent of host immunity.
